Table 8.2:Comparative analysis of the applications of EAs in various fields.

| Application || Description |
| --- | --- |
| Optimization of neural networks || Evolutionary algorithms optimize the architecture, hyperparameters, and weights of neural networks to improve performance in classification, regression, and image recognition tasks. |
| --- | --- |
| Function optimization || Evolutionary algorithms excel in optimizing complex, nonlinear, and multimodal functions, finding global optima where traditional gradient-based methods may struggle. |
| Multi-objective optimization || Evolutionary multi-objective optimization algorithms efficiently generate a set of Pareto-optimal solutions, enabling decision-makers to explore trade-offs between conflicting objectives in diverse applications. |
| Feature selection || Evolutionary algorithms identify subsets of features that maximize predictive performance while minimizing dimensionality, enhancing model interpretability and efficiency in tasks such as classification and regression. |
| Combinatorial optimization || Evolutionary algorithms efficiently solve combinatorial optimization problems like the traveling salesman problem, job scheduling, and vehicle routing by exploring large solution spaces to find optimal or near-optimal solutions. |

## 8.6 Challenges and Future Directions

The key challenges and future directions of EAs are as follows.

### 8.6.1 Challenges

Electronic arts are a very intriguing field of study. Several open research problems include managing the trade-off between exploration and exploitation properties, implementing self-adaptive control of steering parameters, minimizing the number of parameters in the CMA-ES algorithm, developing new selection schemes, and enhancing their efficacy. The latter is very significant, particularly in the domain of design that evolves and evolvable hardware. Furthermore, there is a need for novel and more effective approaches to handle constraints \[[46](#9783111436050_022667.xhtml#b_9783111436180-008_ref_046)\].

Furthermore, further research is needed to explore the use of EAs in dynamic optimization issues, optimization in noisy and non-stationary settings, and multi-objective optimization problems, particularly those with a high number of choice factors. Additionally, additional investigation is required to understand how population size adapts in various optimization settings. To address costly issues more effectively, it is necessary to devise innovative approaches that may enhance competitiveness. One of the issues that must be addressed is how to handle constraints in EAs \[[47](#9783111436050_022667.xhtml#b_9783111436180-008_ref_047)\] when applied to engineering optimization problems. The constraint handling methods can be categorized into six main groups: penalty methods, methods operating within the feasible region, methods employing parallel approaches as the population gets closer, methods assuming the superiority of feasible individuals, techniques utilizing multi-objective optimization techniques, and hybrid methods. Naturally, each of these categories may be further subdivided into several subcategories.

The categorization of the methods used to handle constraints using EAs may be found in \[[48](#9783111436050_022667.xhtml#b_9783111436180-008_ref_048)\]. To implement the appropriate constraint-managing method in EAs for real-world applications, it is necessary to address several questions. These include determining whether the objective function is defined in the infeasible domain (as penalization techniques cannot be used in such cases) and identifying the presence of any active limitations at the optimum. If the approaches based on the search of feasible area borders are not applicable, it is important to determine the nature of the limitations. If there is just one nonlinear inequality constraint, the approaches for linear constraints are not applicable.

Furthermore, in the practical use of EAs with constraint management approaches, the efficacy of a method is sometimes overshadowed by two additional choice criteria: complexity and implementation difficulties. Penalty techniques, feasibility criteria, and stochastic ranking algorithms are often used in real-world applications owing to their inherent simplicity. Thus, it is evident that there is no universal method for managing constraints using EAs that can effectively address every real-world situation. Consequently, the investigation of constraint management approaches in EAs for real-world applications remains a current and important area of study.

It is crucial to possess a comprehensive understanding of the powers and limits of EAs before employing them for optimization purposes. By examining the time it takes to optimize different versions of EAs to solve specific optimization issues, valuable insights may be obtained into the factors that determine the level of difficulty for these problem-solving methods. The creation of methodologies that permit thorough investigation and enable academics to generate answers for new versions of EAs with increasingly complicated issues is more significant than the production of those specific outcomes. [Table 8.3](#9783111436050_022667.xhtml#b_9783111436180-008_tab_003) presents a comparative analysis of the key challenges of EAs in various fields \[[49](#9783111436050_022667.xhtml#b_9783111436180-008_ref_049)\].

Table 8.3:Comparative analysis of key challenges of EAs in various fields.

| Challenge || Description |
| --- | --- |
| Computational complexity || EAs often demand substantial computational resources, particularly for problems featuring large search spaces or intricate fitness evaluations. This complexity can impede efficiency, limiting scalability and practical application in resource-constrained environments. |
| --- | --- |
| Exploration versus exploitation balance || EAs must delicately balance exploration (discovering new regions) and exploitation (exploiting known promising solutions) within the search space. Failure to strike this balance adequately can lead to premature convergence or stagnation, hindering the algorithm’s ability to discover optimal or diverse solutions effectively. |
| Limited adaptability || EAs may struggle to adapt to shifting problem dynamics, constraints, or characteristics, impacting their ability to navigate complex and dynamic optimization landscapes. Enhanced adaptability is crucial to ensure EAs can effectively respond to changes and maintain optimal performance across varied problem contexts. |
| Overfitting and generalization || EAs face the risk of overfitting, wherein they excessively tailor solutions to the training data or search space, potentially compromising performance on unseen data or new problem instances. Robust generalization capabilities are essential to mitigate overfitting and ensure reliable performance in real-world applications. |
| Scalability || Scalability refers to EAs‘ capability to handle increasingly complex or large-scale optimization problems efficiently. Challenges arise when dealing with high-dimensional search spaces, computationally intensive fitness evaluations, or tasks requiring parallelization. Addressing scalability concerns necessitates designing algorithms that can scale effectively without compromising performance or convergence. |

### 8.6.2 Future Directions

As shown in this study \[[50](#9783111436050_022667.xhtml#b_9783111436180-008_ref_050)\], EAs constitute a well-studied field of research. Every year, several novel variations of the algorithms, as mentioned above, are suggested. If a certain issue does not have a suitable specialized algorithm, using one of the EA might be a favorable option. It is important to consider the challenges that users may encounter while working with EAs. Here, we may identify two primary issues. The primary issue at hand is premature convergence, which refers to the population converging toward a suboptimal solution rather than an ideal one. To address this issue, we may implement a system that reduces the pace at which genetic material is transferred between individuals. This can be achieved by dividing the whole population into many subpopulations, sometimes referred to as “islands,” and occasionally allowing individuals to move between these islands \[[51](#9783111436050_022667.xhtml#b_9783111436180-008_ref_051)\].

An alternative approach to address the issue of early convergence involves combining EAs using a branch and bound method, which is enhanced by intermediate propagation approaches. The second issue is the ideal balance between exploring and profiting from the characteristics of EA. Controlling the degree of selection pressure is one possible answer to this issue. This can be achieved by incorporating specialized genetic operators that ensure a high level of population differences at the beginning of the algorithm’s operation (with a strong emphasis on exploration rather than exploitation) and a low level of population variety at the completion of the algorithm’s functioning (with a greater focus on exploitation rather than exploration) \[[52](#9783111436050_022667.xhtml#b_9783111436180-008_ref_052)\].

Future developments in EAs may be highlighted in many key directions. One contemporary approach is the hybrid of multiple algorithms to achieve improved outcomes. Presently, there is a growing body of literature that features a rising number of works showcasing hybrid algorithms. In addition, several researchers are engaged in enhancing the computing efficiency of EAs through various changes. Another intriguing area for future study in EAs is memetic algorithms. The phrase “memetic algorithm” refers to the combination of an evolutionary approach and any additional population-based strategy with independent local search strategies, such as the Nelder-Mead method. Valuable insights into future developments in EAs may be obtained \[[53](#9783111436050_022667.xhtml#b_9783111436180-008_ref_053)\].

One of the upcoming trends in EAs is the growing interest in using EAs for embodied or embedded systems. This means using evolution to create populations of controls and individuals that apply the operational approach for certain situated entities. These solutions are evaluated based on their performance in complex and dynamic surroundings, focusing on their functionality rather than their inherent qualities. In addition, there is another significant concern, particularly in the industrial use of EA techniques. Frequently, while dealing with practical situations, we encounter the need to optimize a function inside a domain that has many dimensions \[[54](#9783111436050_022667.xhtml#b_9783111436180-008_ref_054)\]. This method is often intricate and time-consuming. Thus, in practical scenarios, the EAs developed for such issues must be constructed to be readily implemented in parallel (or GPU-friendly) to minimize their computing time. Future proposals should prioritize a more substantial effort in developing this feature since it has the potential to be a decisive factor in determining the usefulness of an algorithm in practical applications. Research in the field of EAs often involves the use of surrogate models, which are computationally less expensive models of real-world situations. These surrogate models may be used instead of doing complete fitness assessments and can be improved by sometimes evaluating individuals in the population \[[55](#9783111436050_022667.xhtml#b_9783111436180-008_ref_055)\].

Furthermore, it is rather common for industrial challenges to include many goals. Interactive EAs are used with algorithmic advancements to enhance the effectiveness of EAs in multi-objective optimization. It is well understood that a distinct objective function characterizes every engineering issue and has a unique search space topography. The optimal settings of EA parameters that are effective in solving one issue may not be enough for solving another one. [Table 8.4](#9783111436050_022667.xhtml#b_9783111436180-008_tab_004) presents a comparative analysis of future directions and their advantages, as well as challenges.

Table 8.4:Comparative analysis of future directions, their advantages, and challenges.

| Future directions || Description || Advantages || Challenges |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hybridization of methods || This involves merging EAs with other optimization techniques, like swarm intelligence or traditional methods. It aims to leverage the strengths of each approach to overcome individual limitations. || 

*   Synergizes multiple optimization paradigms – enhances exploration and exploitation capabilities – improves solution quality and convergence speed
    

 || 

*   Complexity in integrating different algorithms – finding optimal combinations of methods – potential increase in computational overhead
    

 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Adaptive meta-heuristic || This approach entails developing EAs with adaptive mechanisms. These mechanisms dynamically adjust algorithm parameters, operators, or strategies based on problem characteristics and optimization progress. || 

*   Enhances adaptability to problem dynamics and complexities – improves convergence speed and solution quality – reduces the risk of premature convergence
    

 || 

*   Designing effective adaptation mechanisms – balancing between exploration and exploitation dynamically – ensuring stability and robustness of adaptive algorithms
    

 |
| Diversity preservation || This strategy focuses on maintaining diversity within the population during optimization. It promotes the exploration of diverse regions in the search space and mitigates the risk of premature convergence. || 

*   Enhances exploration of the search space – Reduces risk of premature convergence – improves robustness and solution quality
    

 || 

*   Designing effective diversity maintenance mechanisms – balancing diversity and convergence objectives – ensuring computational efficiency and scalability of diversity-preserving techniques
    

 |

Consequently, the exploration of novel methodologies in the field of automated tuning and adaptive parameter control remains a prominent subject in the realm of EAs. A crucial concern in the commercial implementation of EA techniques is the precise specification of an objective function. The industrial difficulties are quite intricate. Hence, formulating a precise mathematical model (with a well-defined goal function for EAs) for a specific industrial process is an arduous undertaking.

The effectiveness of the selected goal function will significantly impact the outcomes achieved via the use of EA techniques. The last issue we need to address pertains to the replicability of the EA methodologies. It is well understood that EAs are stochastic methods. Every time the EA technique is executed, a distinct outcome may be achieved. Hence, it is crucial to prioritize the establishment of consistent outcomes produced by EA methodologies. This matter has significant importance for the implementation of EA approaches in the industry \[21\].

## 8.7 Conclusion

The real world presents several optimization situations characterized by different limitations and function objectives that exhibit discontinuity, nonlinearity, non-convexity, and multimodality. The optimization issues are complex and include variables of diverse kinds, including integer, real, independent, and binary. These variables have varying ranges of values, which necessitates the use of normalization. Therefore, the problem’s search space lacks smoothness. EAs are increasingly being recognized and used in computer processes to address intricate engineering challenges. They are used by research scientists as well as engineers to utilize the idea of evolution to solve optimization-based investigations and to compose papers. This chapter covers a comprehensive overview of EAs, their applications, challenges, and future directions.

# 9 Introduction to Mathematical Optimization Techniques in AI

Uppuluri Lakshmi Soundharya Yogesh Kumar Sharma Anantha Raman Ravi Rastogi 

#### Abstract

Particularly, real-life problems are progressively complicated and demand more advanced mathematical algorithms and models, which can efficiently handle vast data volumes and identify the best remedies. However, it is important to keep in mind that there is no ideal technique or algorithm since each one possesses certain constraints that can be alleviated or eradicated through the integration of diverse approaches. The field of artificial intelligence (AI) has seen a significant transformation because of the advancements in deep learning (DL) and machine learning (ML). These advancements have enabled the accomplishment of complex tasks such as image recognition and processing natural language with remarkable proficiency. Optimization strategies are essential to building DL and ML models as they provide optimal convergence and improved efficiency. Individuals can optimize existing DL models by using the mathematical principles and derivations that define these approaches. This chapter presents an overview of mathematical optimization techniques in AI, types of optimization methods, their applications, challenges, and future directions.

Keywords:  Mathematical optimization,  AI,  deep learning,  machine learning,  

## 9.1 Introduction

Mathematical algorithms are widely used in a variety of scientific disciplines to resolve challenges. The algorithms, as mentioned earlier, simplify reality using mathematical formulas, allowing us to understand complex procedures, solve difficulties, and make informed decisions. Mathematical algorithms employ techniques to determine the best solution to a given problem. Numerical optimization is a recognized field in mathematics that focuses on identifying the highest and lowest points of an activity \[[1](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_001)\]. The development of optimization strategies has been necessary for various key aspects, which include administration, decision-making, technological advancements, and overall system development in recent decades, offering profitable, positive aspects \[[2](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_002)\].

Mathematical optimization involves formulating a business concern using a number of formulas and analysing them to get the most favourable business outcomes. These equations serve as a framework for thinking and may be repeatedly optimized using various data sources and goals, such as maximizing income, minimizing cost, and achieving a desired service level. Every outcome represents an optimal situation that the user may access and use in the company to have a significant effect \[[3](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_003)\].

Machine learning (ML) is a renowned field that specializes in addressing issues via the use of mathematical frameworks and techniques. Many real-world situations need the processing of large amounts of facts and figures. To convert the unprocessed details into useful information towards solving a problem, this quantity of statistical information often needs statistical support. ML techniques are quite valuable in this particular application. The goal of these procedures and models is to provide a mathematical framework that characterizes the data collection and extrapolates the information to unidentified data sampling. ML algorithms and models are applicable in several fields, such as the business world, health, finance, education, and medical sectors \[[4](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_004)\].

Considering the practical significance of these domains, multiple techniques were created to address optimization with ML difficulties. While most artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms are effective in tackling the issues they encounter, none are flawless. The available research specifies many constraints concerning both optimization and AI strategies. However, in recent years, a number of investigators have begun to explore methods to integrate both approaches to address the limitations of each approach, enhancing processes influenced by additional techniques. These combined approaches are known as hybrids \[[5](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_005)\].

The chapter is organized into various sections, which are as follows: Section 9.2 covers optimization in AI and mathematical optimization techniques, Section 9.3 covers the applications of optimization, Section 9.4 covers challenges and future directions of optimization, and the final section covers the conclusion of the research.

## 9.2 Mathematical Optimization and AI Algorithms

According to Gartner research, AI is a field of computer science and engineering that employs mathematical and logical procedures to extract and incorporate programming expertise. It utilizes advanced and intelligent processes to solve issues, understand events, facilitate decision-making, and perform automated operations \[[6](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_006)\]. Gartner classifies AI into three primary classifications:

*   Optimization techniques (OT)
    
*   Computational logic (CL)
    
*   Probabilistic reasoning (PR)
    

![Figure 9.1: Types of mathematical optimization techniques.](graphic/converted/b_9783111436180-009_fig_001.png)

Figure 9.1: Types of mathematical optimization techniques.

Optimization approaches include several methods, such as linear programming, which concentrates on “linear objective functions” and rules; nonlinear programming, which is utilized for nonlinear functions; linear programming with integers for individual factors; and dynamic programming, which is used for issues with overlapping subdivisions. [Figure 9.1](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_fig_001) presents the types of mathematical OTs \[[7](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_007)\]. Mathematical optimization and AI are distinct AI methodologies. However, there is frequent confusion between the two. AI algorithms support ML and deep learning (DL) algorithms in mathematical optimization-based problem-solving. ML is primarily concerned with making predictions and calculating probabilities, while mathematical optimization is a prescriptive method that aims to determine a practical path of action. While ML forecasts might guide specific choices, ML is not inherently capable of addressing complex business situations that include several linked factors. This is where optimization really shines. A crucial distinction between ML and optimization lies in the fact that optimization begins with the business issue as the primary focus rather than the data \[[14](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_014), [15](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_015)\].

Accessible data significantly influences the outcomes of an ML algorithm. It is often necessary to evaluate these outcomes by comparing them against extensive volumes of data to ensure accuracy. This entails examining not only a mere ten thousand items in a file but also occasionally millions of records. ML models may present challenges when it comes to adapting to changing business circumstances or demands because of their heavy reliance on past data. This reduces their flexibility. ML models often struggle to handle exceptional cases \[[16](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_016)\].

On the other hand, optimization is especially designed to handle exceptions by explicitly modelling restrictions. The variables involved in the decision-making process, as well as their interconnections, should be clearly defined regardless of the available data. Proficiency in business logic is required. Consequently, the process of creating an optimization model may require a longer initial investment. However, after you possess a model, you may effortlessly broaden its scope and experiment with novel concepts to operate the organization, for instance, including restrictions to limit the number of suppliers, specifically establishing safety thresholds for inventories, mandating a minimum decrease in CO[2] emissions, and so on. Moreover, it is possible to increase the quantity of goals. This enables you to comprehend the behaviour of the issue when subjected to various objectives, including the optimization of several objectives, often known as multi-objective optimization \[[17](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_017)\].

## 9.3 Optimization Problem-Solving Framework

Although there are many approaches and techniques available for addressing issues associated with optimization, only a few of them can be considered universally applicable or flawless in their ability to efficiently handle all such difficulties. Typically, each method encounters distinct features that make it more suited for solving a certain group of issues based on its unique qualities. To solve an optimization issue, it is important to consider the problem creation, methodologies, and algorithm selection. This is because various methods and approaches work better for different types of problems \[[18](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_018)\].

A mathematical framework formulation is the initial stage in solving a problem related to optimization. The goal of a mathematical framework is to translate a real-world issue into a mathematical equation that OTs can utilize. An effort to optimize problems may be mathematically formulated using a collection of data points and mathematical relationships that provide an abstract representation of the problem. The goal is to identify the best possible alternative, known as the optimum solution, from a given set of candidate solutions. To construct a mathematical framework, one must adhere to four phases \[[19](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_019)\]:

*   Step 1: Decision variable declaration and initialization, i.e., (DC[1], DC[2], … DC[*n*]).
    
*   Step 2: Create a recursive decision function f (DC) using the decision variables.
    
*   Where *f*(*D**C*) = *B**e**s**t*( *f*1(*D**C*), *f*2(*D**C*),  …  …  …  … *f**n*(*D**C*))
    
*   Step 3: To hold the decision variables, define some constraints and conditions of equality and inequality.
    
*   Step 4: Define the characteristics of the problem domain (Pd[1], Pd[2], … Pd*[n]*).
    

The optimization issue is defined by the objective function as well as the restrictions imposed on the variables that are involved. The function that defines the objective represents the goal for the problem, and this is composed of an individual and grouping of numbers which are convertible to just one value, such as individuals, time, goods, resources, etc. On the other hand, the obstacles directly impact the space of decisions and outcomes, imposing restrictions and constraints upon the procedure’s selections.

The primary purpose of an optimization issue is to reduce and optimize the objective function while taking into account the restrictions. Furthermore, a potential approach to categorize optimization models based on the number of goals is to split them into two main categories: single-objective and multi-objective planning associated with optimization. Multi-objective optimization represents a branch of multiple criteria decision-making makes decisions that involves multiple goals, and each function must be maximized concurrently, even when there are restrictions. Single-objective optimization problems typically include one objective that must be maximized, with or without restrictions. Once the mathematical model has been developed, it is crucial to select the most suitable strategy for finding the optimum answer \[[20](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_020)\].

The concepts of both local and global optimizations may characterize the answer to an optimization issue. Similarly, the search techniques can be categorized as local search as well as global search. Algorithms for both local and global optimization of search results are used differently or to address distinct optimization problems. Local optimization involves identifying a solution that reduces or maximizes the objective function within a defined area of the search space. This implies that it focuses on finding a solution that is locally optimal among viable locations within the nearby vicinity. This particular type of search does not ensure an objective value that is lower or greater than all other possible points.

In contrast, global optimization aims to identify the optimal point that minimizes or maximizes the objective function across all viable solutions. Nevertheless, the intricacy of global OTs increases exponentially as the issues get larger \[[21](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_021), [22](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_022)\]. [Table 9.2](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_tab_002) presents a comparative analysis of the optimization framework for various mathematical optimization methods.

The process begins with an initial population of randomly generated solutions and progresses through successive generations towards improved solutions. || Global optimization handles non-differentiable and discontinuous functions and has parallel processing capabilities. || The rate of convergence may be sluggish, and there may be a high level of complexity in setting the parameters. || Areas of expertise include engineering design, allocation of resources, and evolutionary automation. |

Optimization involves the use of several strategies and algorithms to discover the answer to a problem. Certain optimization approaches exhibit unique characteristics while searching for an approach to the same issue, resulting in some methods being quicker and more dependable in terms of accuracy compared to others. There is no universal approach to efficiently handle all optimization issues. Instead, we have several methods that can potentially be used within their respective capacities to address issues associated with optimization.

## 9.4 Mathematical Optimization Techniques

Mathematical optimization, often known as mathematical programming, involves choosing the most optimal element from a given collection of possibilities based on certain criteria. Typically, it is categorized into a pair of subdivisions: discrete optimization and continuous optimization. Numerical optimization is a branch of mathematics that focuses on finding the highest and lowest boundaries of operations. Over the past couple of decades, there has been an increase in curiosity about optimization approaches, mostly driven by advancements in computing technology and their widespread uses. Therefore, the implementation of OTs is increasingly becoming a crucial instrument for supervisors, decision-making processes, enhancement, and advancement of innovations to facilitate the operation of systems that operate effectively. The general framework represents concerns by using decision parameters, which are constants that individuals have control over and can adjust as knobs. \[[29](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_029)\].

Mathematical optimization is often referred to as “mathematical programming.” The term is frequently used synonymously with predictive analytics, also known as an instance of analytics that generates an advisable plan of action. Mathematical optimization is frequently recognized as the most prominent method for prescriptive analysis in the industry. Prescriptive analytics differs from descriptive and predictive analytics in that it provides recommendations on how business processes should be improved or evolved rather than simply reporting trends or forecasting the future \[[30](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_030)\].

Prescriptive analytics is essential for transforming data and business rules into meaningful measures rather than just offering insights into the behaviour of that information. In addition to its role as a prescriptive analytics tool, mathematical optimization is also regarded as a kind of computational intelligence (CI). Constraints refer to limitations or restrictions placed on the possible values that the decision variables may have. Perhaps the goal function(s) are the ones we want to optimize. The key types of mathematical optimization methods are as follows.

### 9.4.1 Gradient Descent

This is a key optimization method employed in the field of AI. The objective is to minimize a cost function by constantly adjusting the variables of the mathematical framework using the change in gradients and the cost function compared to the relevant variables \[[31](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_031)\].

*   **Mathematical Formulation:** Considering a neural network, its parameters are denoted by the symbol *θ*. The goal is to minimize a function of costs *J*(*θ*), which evaluates the efficiency of the mathematical framework. The derivative of *J*(*θ*) in relation to *θ* is represented as ∇*J*(*θ*). The modification phase in a gradient descent (GD) is often formally represented as follows:
    

(9.1)*θ* = ((*θ*−*α*) \* ∇*J*(*θ*)) 

In this context, the symbol *α*, also known as the learning rate (LR), determines the magnitude of the adjustment made to the parameters. It plays a crucial role in determining the pace at which the optimization process converges and the stability it achieves.

### 9.4.2 Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)

SGD involves a modified version of GD, which calculates the gradients and then adjusts the setting parameters by employing a small subset of the training specimens, known as a mini-batch, instead of the complete dataset. This strategy significantly decreases the computing load and accelerates the optimization process \[[32](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_032)\].

**Mathematical Formulation:** Let a small group of training samples be called *B*, including the total cost function *J*(*θ*), as previously mentioned. The revision step in SGD is

(9.2)*θ* = \[*θ*−{*α* \* ∇*J*(*θ*; *B*)}) 

In this case, ∇*J*(*θ*; *B*) denotes the gradient for *J*(*θ*) calculated for mini-batch *B*.

### 9.4.3 Momentum Optimization

GD represents an optimization procedure that finds the function’s absolute optimum by following the objective function’s unfavourable gradient. When used to optimize problems with high degrees of curvature and unpredictable gradients, GD is employed. A GD method tends to bounce around the search space until it becomes stuck in areas within the search space devoid of gradients.

An expansion of the GD optimization technique is the momentum algorithm, which enables the search to generate energy in a particular direction within the search space, thereby overcoming the disturbances caused by chaotic gradients and traversing the space’s smooth areas along the coast \[[33](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_033)\].

More exactly, momentum may be defined as the moving average of prior gradients weighted exponentially. The optimizer uses the exponentially weighted moving average of the prior gradients to update the parameters rather than using the current gradient. The optimizer can remember its previous path and stick to it even if the gradient is pointing in the opposite direction, thanks to an exponentially weighted moving average, which acts as a memory.

It is common practice to use momentum with other optimization techniques, including SGD as well as adaptive learning rate (ALR) techniques like Adam (AD), Adagrad (ADG), and Adadelta (ADD). The momentum algorithm incorporates a momentum element into the procedure for updating to overcome the drawbacks of GD. Momentum, defined with the characteristics of a “ball going downhill,” is a portion of the previous revision of the vector. Despite the event that the gradient reverses course or becomes zero, the momentum factor keeps the optimizer moving in the same path as it descends. This lowers oscillations and prevents us from entering shallow neighbourhood minima \[[34](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_034)\]:

(9.3)*V* = {*β**V*+\[(1−*β*)*a**b**l**a*)*θ**J*(*θ*)} (9.4)*θ* = \[*θ*−*α**v*) 

In this equation, the variable *V* stands for the momentum term, which is the momentum coefficient, and *J*() is the gradient of the cost function with respect to the parameters, and is the LR. Usually, one sets the momentum coefficient to 0.901. In every iteration, the optimizer determines the cost function’s gradient and updates the momentum term by taking the exponentially weighted moving average of the prior gradients. The momentum term multiplied by the LR is then subtracted to update the parameters \[[35](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_035)\].

### 9.4.4 Adam Optimization

The algorithm known as Adam optimizer is an incremental optimization technique employed to minimize the loss function throughout the development of neural networks. This is an abbreviation for “adaptive moment estimation (AME).” When considering momentum, Adam is often conceptualized as a hybrid of SGD and RMSprop (RMp); Diederik-p created this method.

The method uses the squared gradients to adjust the LR in a manner similar to RMSprop. Additionally, it leverages momentum by employing the average movement of the gradient rather than the gradient of its own, comparable to SGD alongside momentum. This approach combines the use of a dynamic learning rate (DLR) with easing techniques to effectively attain the global minimum \[[36](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_036)\]. The following Adam setup variables are used in the configurations.

*   Alpha: The term “learning rate,” also called “step size,” is used interchangeably to refer to this concept. The weight change percentage, denoted as 0.001, determines the extent to which weights are adjusted. Higher numbers (such as 0.3) lead to quicker learning processes until the rate is adjusted. Lower values (such as 1.0E-5) significantly decrease the speed of learning throughout the training.
    
*   Beta one: For initial moment estimates, an exponential decay rate (such as 0.9) is used.
    
*   Beta two: The speed at which the second-moment estimations decrease exponentially is 0.999. The recommended value for issues with a sparse gradient, such as NLP as well as computer vision tasks, is about 1.0.
    
*   Epsilon: To avoid dividing by zero in the operation, an extremely tiny number (such as 10E-8) is used.
    

## 9.5 Applications

Mathematical optimization, particularly optimization modelling, may provide solutions to any of these inquiries. This approach involves the process of expressing a business challenge using mathematical formulas or equations. It metaphorically represents the choices you must make, the limitations you must adhere to, and the interconnections between them to accomplish a certain goal. “A mathematical model" is the term used to explain such business logic. The key application of mathematical optimization is as follows \[[37](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_037), [38](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_038)\].

Capacity Planning (CP): CP involves monitoring and managing network resources on behalf of the NaaS provider. It uses key parameters to forecast the network’s behaviour and schedules actions to increase capacity when needed. In the context of operations management, CP represents the process of harmonizing consumer demand for a particular good or business service alongside an organization’s or manufacturer’s ability to produce sufficient quantities to satisfy that demand.

Healthcare Systems (HS): This area of expertise uses the IBM CPLEX solvers to tackle linear programming challenges using high-speed programming for mathematical techniques. Mathematical modelling is used to simulate and analyse clinical studies. IBM CPLEX is a software tool for decision optimization that facilitates the creation and implementation of optimization models. The field of cancer research has used mathematical OTs since the beginning of the twentieth century, which have been applied to advancements in the field of medicine.

Energy Systems (ESs): In the field of ESs, an objective measure refers to the amount of energy utilized by a system. The purpose of the energy framework is to minimize energy use. The energy management system’s (EMS) efficiency and effectiveness are contingent upon the energy management strategy (EMS) and forecast algorithms employed. Traditional power grids use several techniques, such as fuzzy logic, the theory of games, and learning through reinforcement in their energy administration systems. The application of fuzzy logic in EMS is effective in optimizing operating costs. At the same time, the use of game theory in EMS is effective in lowering overall power consumption and the associated costs of emissions in the ES.

Supply Chain Network Design (SCND): The supply chain comprises manufacturing facilities, storage facilities, distribution centres, and client regions. The issue involves concurrent operational and financial choices, hence requiring appropriate variables as well as parameters in its mathematical formulation. The suggested model focuses on the supply chain network. The logistics chain comprises manufacturing facilities, storage facilities, centres for distribution, and client regions. The issue involves both operational and financial choices concurrently, necessitating the use of appropriate parameterized variables in the mathematical equation. The suggested model takes into account the supply chain network.

In electrical engineering, optimization methods are often used for several purposes. These involve designing active filters, reducing stray fields in the storage of superconducting magnetic ESs, designing microwave constructions using space in the mapping process, and designing handset antennas utilizing electromagnetic radiation. ## 9.6 Challenges and Future Directions

The key challenges and future directions of mathematical optimization methods are as follows.

### 9.6.1 Challenges

Optimization strategies are very beneficial, but their successful implementation is not always simple or direct.

*   The effectiveness of an optimization strategy is directly dependent on the quality of its formulation. Although it may be theoretically accurate, it might still be of little practical use.
    
*   Frequently, several comparable formulations are available, which vary significantly in terms of effectiveness and solutions. Choosing relevant descriptions requires a moderate level of experience.
    
*   Optimization strategies are limited to the information they are provided. The conceptual framework must include every relevant component of the intended solution, whether it is implied or stated directly (such as optimum control learning).
    

### 9.6.2 Future Directions

In the future, this study has the potential for further inquiry and progress in other interesting avenues. Continued research and development in hybrid optimization methodology are necessary. This includes investigating new hybridization strategies, adaptive learning mechanisms, and ensemble approaches to improve the efficacy and adaptability of optimization algorithms. Additionally, future research endeavours need to prioritize the resolution of new obstacles in optimization. These problems include effectively managing uncertainty, integrating domain-specific expertise, and optimizing for many competing goals in intricate decision-making situations. This entails investigating resilient optimization methods, multi-objective optimization frameworks, and hybrid optimization paradigms designed for particular application domains and issue situations \[[39](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_039), [40](#9783111436050_024552.xhtml#b_9783111436180-009_ref_040)\].

Furthermore, there is an increasing potential for interdisciplinary cooperation and exchange of ideas among optimization academics and practitioners from many domains, such as data science, AI, and systems engineering. By promoting interdisciplinary conversation and the sharing of information, we may use ideas from several disciplines to create innovative optimization approaches and successfully tackle real-world difficulties. In addition, this study has the potential to expand into the creation of optimization tools and software platforms that prioritize the needs of users. These tools would provide stakeholders with user-friendly interfaces, interactive visualization tools, and customizable processes to aid in problem-solving and decision-making. By making advanced optimization capabilities accessible to everyone, we can enable individuals and organizations in various sectors to utilize mathematical optimization to promote innovation and generate positive societal outcomes.

Ultimately, this study acts as a foundation for fully harnessing the capabilities of mathematical optimization to tackle intricate real-world issues and shape a future that is more effective, adaptable, and environmentally friendly. By adopting multidisciplinary teamwork, innovation in technology, and user-centric design principles, we can pave the way for significant progress in solving optimization-driven problems and making decisions. This will lead to the exploration of new areas in the discovery of information, innovation, and the well-being of society. ## 9.7 Conclusion

This study has conducted an extensive investigation of mathematical optimization strategies, including both traditional approaches and contemporary metaheuristic algorithms that are computationally efficient. It also covers their types, applications, and challenges. The survey covers a broad range of optimization methods utilized in diverse fields, including AI, ML, and programming in mathematics. The study examines the intrinsic difficulties encountered by current algorithms, such as problems with flexibility, speed of integration, and capacity to adapt to various application domains.

Mathematical optimization has practical uses in several sectors and areas. It offers a groundbreaking technique for tackling intricate challenges and making choices. Mathematical OTs have proven to be helpful resources for companies, government agencies, and investigators. The techniques can be applied to various areas such as producing goods, transportation, logistics, supply chain management, healthcare administration, and handling financial hazards.

# 10 Hybrid Mathematical Optimization Techniques in AI

Umesh Kumar Lilhore Sarita Simaiya Surjeet Dalal 

#### Abstract

This chapter covers hybrid mathematical optimization techniques in artificial intelligence (AI) to overcome local minima and slow convergence. Hybrid methods improve performance and robustness by combining multiple optimization strategies. The chapter divides hybridization into serial, parallel, and adaptive methods. Serial hybridization uses genetic algorithms (GA) for broad exploration and gradient descent for fine-tuning. Multiple algorithms run simultaneously in parallel hybridization, improving search diversity and robustness. Problem characteristics drive adaptive hybridization strategy adjustments. GA with gradient descent for neural network training, PSO with simulated annealing (SA) for complex optimization, and DE with local search for enhanced exploration and exploitation are examined. Practical applications show how hybrid techniques improve neural network training, hyperparameter optimization, feature selection, and robotics path planning. These methods work in real life, as shown by case studies. Finally, the chapter emphasizes hybrid optimization in AI and suggests future research on developing more adaptive algorithms and integrating them with deep learning to create robust and efficient solutions.

Keywords:  Hybrid mathematical optimization techniques,  artificial intelligence,  genetic algorithms,  PSO,  simulated annealing,  

## 10.1 Introduction

Since mathematical models are essential to solving problems, they are found in practically all branches of science. These models offer a condensed depiction of reality based on mathematical expressions. These formulations facilitate problem-solving, the understanding of complex systems, and the acquisition of crucial data to enable wise decision-making. Algorithms are used by mathematical models to determine the best solution for the given problem \[[1](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_ref_001)\]. The goal of the well-known mathematical science field of numerical optimization is to pinpoint a function’s extreme points, whether they are its maximum or minimum. Over the past 20 years, optimization techniques have grown in importance as a tool for management, decision-making, technology advancement, and development. They give different systems a competitive edge \[[2](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_ref_002)\].

Artificial intelligence (AI) has changed many fields, such as healthcare, entertainment, finance, and transportation. Among the best things about AI is that it can do things that humans are good at, like understanding language, using logic, learning new things, and solving problems. Optimization is a critical mathematical tool for decision-making and determining the best solutions within a given set of constraints and requirements. AI optimization entails selecting the most efficient solution from a set of available options. Conventional optimization methods such as simulated annealing (SA), genetic algorithms (GA), and gradient descent have been critical in resolving a wide range of AI challenges \[[3](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_ref_003)\].

Gradient descent is commonly employed to locate local minima, especially in the training of neural networks, owing to its simplicity and efficacy. SA, a technique inspired by metallurgical annealing, is highly efficient in circumventing local minima while approximating global optima. GAs, which are based on natural selection, are ideal for solving global search problems. Despite their benefits, traditional methods frequently encounter significant challenges when dealing with the complexities of modern AI applications. Nonconvex functions, large search spaces, constraints, and the presence of multiple local minima are all common challenges. Moreover, the practical effectiveness of these methods is limited by their tendency to converge at a slow pace or get trapped in suboptimal solutions \[[4](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_ref_004)\].

Hybrid mathematical optimization techniques have emerged as a potent alternative to address these obstacles. Hybrid optimization techniques combine two or more optimization methods, utilizing their individual strengths to compensate for their weaknesses. The primary objective of hybridization is to enhance the robustness, accuracy, and convergence speed of the optimization process. Serial hybridization, parallel hybridization, and adaptive hybridization are the three primary types of hybrid optimization techniques \[[5](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_ref_005)\].

Significantly, actual problems are progressively intricate and necessitate advanced models and algorithms that can efficiently handle extensive data sets and identify optimal solutions. Nevertheless, it is important to note that no method or algorithm can be considered flawless, as they all possess certain limitations. However, these limitations can be reduced or eradicated by integrating the expertise of various methodologies. The objective is to create hybrid algorithms that can effectively combine the strengths and unique characteristics of optimization and machine learning methods, resulting in improved efficiency \[[6](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_ref_006), [7](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_ref_007)\].

This chapter presents hybrid mathematical optimization techniques in AI to overcome local minima and slow convergence. Hybrid methods improve performance and robustness by combining multiple optimization strategies. The chapter is organized into various sections, which cover the review of existing methods, the importance of hybrid optimization, types, methodologies of hybrid optimization, applications, future directions, and, lastly, the conclusion.

## 10.3 Hybrid Optimization Techniques

Hybrid optimization strategies take advantage of the benefits and minimize the drawbacks of two or more optimization techniques. The benefits of hybridization include increased robustness, accuracy, and speed of convergence. Hybrid AI is a notable breakthrough in the field of AI as it combines two separate approaches: rule-based and machine learning-based techniques. This innovative combination enhances the capability and efficiency of AI systems, surpassing the restrictions of individual rule-based or learning-based approaches. [Table 10.1](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_tab_001) presents a comparative analysis of types of hybrid optimization techniques.

Table 10.1:Comparative analysis of types of hybrid optimization techniques.

| Hybridization technique || Description || Example || Advantages || Challenges |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Serial hybridization || Optimization methods are applied sequentially. || A genetic algorithm (GA) explores the search space broadly, followed by gradient descent for fine-tuning the solution. || Combines the strengths of multiple methods; GA finds global solutions, gradient descent fine-tunes. || Can be time-consuming; requires careful method selection. |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Parallel hybridization || Multiple optimization algorithms run simultaneously, sharing information between them. || Genetic algorithm and particle swarm optimization running in parallel, exchanging best solutions. || Diversifies the search process; helps in escaping local minima. || High computational cost; complexity in managing parallel processes. |
| Adaptive hybridization || Dynamically adjusts the optimization strategy based on the problem’s characteristics and the progress of the search process. || Switching between genetic algorithm and simulated annealing based on search performance. || Adapts to problem dynamics; potentially more efficient solutions. || Requires sophisticated control mechanisms; high complexity. |

### 10.3.1 Methodologies of Hybrid Optimization

Hybrid optimizations involve the dynamic selection of an optimization algorithm at compile time from a collection of different algorithms that achieve the same optimization. They employ a heuristic method to forecast the most suitable algorithm for optimizing each piece of code \[[8](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_ref_008)\]. Different optimization methods and algorithms can be used in optimization to identify the solution to the problem. Some optimization techniques show different behavior in the search for the solution to the same problem; thus, one method can be faster and more dependable in response accuracy than others. [Table 10.2](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_tab_002) presents a comparative analysis of methodologies in hybridization optimization, and [Figure 10.1](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_fig_001) presents the flowchart of hybrid optimization methods.

| Hybridization technique || Description || Example || Advantages || Challenges |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Genetic algorithm and gradient descent \[[8](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_ref_008)\] || Combining GA with gradient descent is effective, as GA provides a good initial solution, and gradient descent refines it to a local optimum. || Useful in neural network training, where GA finds a good starting point and gradient descent fine-tunes the weights. || Combines the global search capability of GA with the fine-tuning ability of gradient descent; results in better local optima. || Requires careful parameter tuning; GA can be computationally expensive. |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Particle swarm optimization and simulated annealing \[[9](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_ref_009)\] || PSO is good at global search but may get stuck in local optima. Combining PSO with SA, which has a better capability of escaping local optima, can yield better results. || Suitable for complex optimization problems where PSO finds promising areas, and SA refines the solution by escaping local minima. || Enhances the ability to escape local minima; combines the global exploration of PSO with the local refinement of SA. || High computational cost; requires managing interactions between PSO and SA. |
| Differential evolution and local search \[[10](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_ref_010)\] || DE is effective for global optimization, while local search techniques can exploit the neighborhood of the current best solution. || Used in scenarios where DE explores the global search space, and local search techniques enhance solution accuracy by exploiting nearby solutions. || Balances global exploration of DE with local exploitation; improves both exploration and exploitation capabilities. || Complexity in coordinating DE with local search methods; may require significant computational resources. |

Many algorithms nowadays are developed with different strengths and weaknesses, none of which is the best for every situation. Although they are rather general ideas with many uses, separate and combined, optimization and deep learning \[[11](#9783111436050_026657.xhtml#b_9783111436180-010_ref_011)\]. ## 10.6 Conclusion

We have explored the revolutionary field of hybrid mathematical optimization techniques in this chapter, which are powerful allies when dealing with challenging AI problems. Through the integration of distinct advantages from different optimization approaches, these strategies not only improve performance but also strengthen resilience and improve the overall efficiency of operations. This chapter conducts a comprehensive literature review concerning hybrid techniques that combine optimization and AI methods.

This comprehensive inquiry has meticulously examined fundamental concepts, methodological intricacies, diverse applications across different fields, and insightful glimpses into future prospects, providing a thorough comprehension of the substantial impact and promising future of hybrid mathematical optimization in the realm of AI. Rapid advancements in the field of artificial intelligence are driving the need for hybrid optimization techniques, which are essential for exploring new possibilities and facilitating significant advancements.
