# 13 Explainable Artificial Intelligence Techniques in Deep Learning-Based Liver Tumor Analysis

R. Manjula Devi S. Dheenathayalan 

#### Abstract

As medical imaging technology develops, artificial intelligence (AI) can help radiologists and physicians classify liver tumors accurately and significantly. However, the inherent intricacy of AI models, primarily deep learning algorithms, commonly precludes their adoption because their decision-making processes are opaque and difficult to explain. This chapter proposes a complete architecture that achieves high classification accuracy and offers interpretable perceptions of the model’s choice, addressing the important requirement for explainable AI in liver tumor classification. The proposed system combines existing deep learning architectures with cutting-edge explainable AI (XAI) XAI methods to produce a hybrid model that syndicates predicted accuracy with understandable validations. The model may concentrate on essential areas of medical images and emphasize discriminative features that contribute to its classification conclusions because the framework implements attention mechanisms and feature visualization techniques.

Keywords:  Model clarification,  convolutional neural networks,  SHapley Additive exPlanations,  local interpretable model-agnostic explanations,  partial dependence plots,  

## 13.1 Introduction

The use of machine learning (ML) algorithms has increased over the past decades because artificial intelligence (AI) has seen tremendous and ongoing advancement. These astounding achievements are closely related to opaque, black-box AI models and increased model complexity proposed by Bakrania et al. \[1\]. It is necessary to develop solutions that can help overcome such a challenge to boost the usage of AI systems in delicate and significant fields like healthcare and security, where extra requirements must be met in addition to high accuracy. AI that can explain its decisions or forecasts to human users is known as explainable AI (XAI). XAI aims to improve the openness, dependability, and accountability of AI systems, mainly when applied in high-risk fields like security, finance, or healthcare. The process used in explainable AI is depicted in [Figure 13.1](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_fig_001). Various methods inspect the liver tumor before the medical data is provided to the XAI framework proposed by Peng et al. \[[2](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_002)\]. The clinicians are then given the proposed XAI technique’s computer-aided diagnostic (CAD) results. Finally, medical professionals use CAD to support the diagnosis and treatment of the liver.

![Figure 13.1: Process of explainable AI.](graphic/converted/b_9783111436180-013_fig_001.png)

Figure 13.1: Process of explainable AI.

The exercise data will be provided as an input in XAI-based techniques. Based on the requirements, the internal workings of the model are developed to describe the workings of the output interface. As a result, XAI’s users are aware of its effects, boosting trust in AI systems. Users can increase the accuracy of the results and reveal model defects based on the understanding of the output, which will help users make the best decision for model improvement. The proposed XAI model is outlined in [Figure 13.2](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_fig_002). To recover the medical understanding of the liver tumor, the proposed paradigm dispenses both global and local explanations.

![Figure 13.2: The outline of XAI.](graphic/converted/b_9783111436180-013_fig_002.png)

Figure 13.2: The outline of XAI.

Data collection and preprocessing are done to acquire the patient records. The model is then loaded to forecast how the exacerbation risk will pan out. The global and local explanations are then obtained using the model explanation technique. The results of the model and the explanation will then be reviewed and further validated by the radiologist.

## 13.2 Literature Review

Ahmed and Shelly \[3\] created a stack-ensemble-based ML model framework using XAI to depict the association between the risk factors for lung cancer and the spatial distribution of LBC. The XAI in the disciplines of drugs, psychology, medical structures, and other areas is explained by \[[4](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_004)\]. However, prognostics and health management (PHM) did not offer the analytical method to decrease patient waiting times, enhance services, boost productivity in telemedicine, and increase accuracy, speed, and efficiency.

Andreu-Perez and Emberson \[[5](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_005)\] created an XAI-based model for investigating the development and functionality of baby brain images captured by near-infrared spectroscopy. Atul Anand and Tushar Kadian \[[6](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_006)\] proposed deep neural networks for identifying heart diseases using ECG signals. Bakrania et al. \[1\] discussed the challenges of AI in liver cancer diagnosis and management. In addition, they discussed the future perspectives of AI application in liver cancer and how a multidisciplinary approach using AI in nanomedicine could accelerate the transition of personalized liver cancer medicine from bench side to the clinic. Kumar et al. \[[7](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_007)\] proposed investigating the applicability of AI techniques in photovoltaic systems. Fang and Tan \[[8](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_008)\] created a model to employ patient characteristics to determine the likelihood that a specific disease would progress. However, they need more transparency in clinical practice.

Introduced a classifier based on the convolutional neural network for finding lashes and outlined the saliency maps used to trace the output of the model. Jahmunah et al. \[[9](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_009)\]have created dense net and CNN models to predict abnormalities in EEG signals. In healthcare applications, AI and ML are crucial, and hence, XAI is employed to earn the conviction of AI models. It will increase confidence in extrapolative models in real-world scenarios.

Conducted research on skin malignancies for both males and females. In their work, biomarkers were used for predicting skin cancer, along with trained XGboost ML models. Jahmunah and Ng \[[11](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_011)\] discussed the ideas and methods of XAI-based cardiology. Kute and Pradhan \[[12](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_012)\] proposed that XAI is characterized by knowledge- and data-based strategies. Knowledge-driven XAI requires knowledge about how to explain, whereas data-driven XAI needs local, global, and instance-specific procedures for explanation. They used the publicly accessible PTB-XL output dataset. XAI explanation was given a new meaning by Merry and Riddle \[13\]. Miro-Nicolau and Moya-Alcover \[[14](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_014)\] observed the results using XAI chest images. X-ray images were represented using class activation maps (CAM) in their work. Obayya and Nemri \[[15](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_015)\] developed XAI approaches in teleophthalmology. The accuracy of the categorization model was 98.24% by utilizing the SPECT MPI pictures. Papandrianos Feleki \[[16](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_016)\] created a deep XAI approach to envisage coronary artery disease (CAD).

Peng and Zou \[[2](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_002)\] proposed a framework combining global and local interpretable methods to improve the transparency of complex models and gain insight into the judgments from these models, thereby guiding treatment strategies and improving the prognosis of hepatitis patients. Pertzborn and Arolt \[[17](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_017)\] presented a VGG 19 model to detect malignancies. In their work, deep learning-based models combined with XAI techniques and preprocessing data led to an accuracy of 80%. According to Lombardi and Diacono \[[18](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_018)\], it is possible to predict Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and cognitive impairment using XAI. The disease has been identified using random forest classifiers. Datasets for monitoring patients' health are gathered from various sources. Some information is collected through sensors, while other data comes directly from clinical trials and other studies proposed by Yang \[19\]. To identify and perceive brain cancers in clinical areas, Zeineldin et al. \[[20](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_ref_020)\] developed an XAI framework in neurology for analyzing brain tumors.

## 13.3 Proposed Methodology

The progress of a CAD system for CT liver diagnosis based on AI has advanced significantly in recent years. Due to the nonlinearity of the clinical data collected from hospitals, deep learning-based models perform better than ML methods. However, radiologists are suspicious of complicated models because they operate like a black box that superintends the reasons behind their decisions. Hence, this chapter proposes an XAI framework to address these problems by providing global and local interpretations of liver tumor diagnoses while maintaining high prediction accuracy. First, the framework’s viability is examined using a public dataset collected from a multispecialty scan center. Both apparent and black-box ML models are used to better the classification performance. Finally, the SHapley Additive exPlanations and partial dependence plots are utilized to enhance the model interpretation of liver tumors. In the proposed system, the data taken from the patient is initially stored in the design and given to the XAI framework for further processing, and the results are again stored in the server. Then, it is fed as an input to the CAD system. Once the results are obtained from the CAD system, the radiologist compares the results obtained from the XAI framework and CAD system. The suggested prototype offers global and local explanations to enhance medical empathy of the risk prediction for liver tumors. Data collection and preparation are used to create patient records. The model is then loaded to forecast how the exacerbation risk will pan out. The global and local explanations are then obtained using the model explanation technique. Doctors receive them to examine and further validate the prediction and explanation outcomes.

### 13.3.1 Dataset Description

In this work, CT abdomen images are obtained from the freely available database ([https://www.ircad.fr/research/data-sets/liver-segmentation-3d-ircadb-01/](https://www.ircad.fr/research/data-sets/liver-segmentation-3d-ircadb-01/)) 3DIRCADB (3D image reconstruction for comparison of algorithm database) and the private dataset obtained from multispecialty scan centres. Compared with the other challenge datasets, the 3DIRCADB dataset has a higher diversity and complexity of livers and lesions. The widely available 3DIRCADB dataset encloses 20 venous phases enhanced CT scans of the liver hepatic tumors of 75% of cases by considering 10 women and 10 men. The dimension of the slice is 511 × 511 pixels, with height and width varying from 0.55 to 0.89 mm and the width between adjacent slices ranging from 1.4 to 5.1 mm. Since the 3DIRCADB dataset offered improved diversity and difficulty of livers and their tumors, it is considered a challenging database.Besides, the dataset collected from the scan center encompasses 130 scans of different patients. A minimum of 84 slices per patient are regarded with the expert segmentations manually provided by the radiologist. These images are obtained from Arthi Scan Center Chennai, Tamilnadu, India.

### 13.3.2 Preprocessing

Preprocessing is a significant phase to enhance image quality and increase image analysis performance. Recently, several denoising techniques have been proposed for removing Gaussian noise. Moreover, numerous 2D wavelet-based denoising methods have also been established to alter the image into multiple subbands at different angles. Then, each subband’s wavelet coefficients are applied to a denoising procedure. These filters effectively smooth the noise but still have difficulty blurring the edges within the images. This work employs a block-based non-local means (NLM) algorithm , median filtering with pixel modelling technique as shown in [Figure 13.3](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_fig_003).

![Figure 13.3: Preprocessing methods.](graphic/converted/b_9783111436180-013_fig_003.png)

Figure 13.3: Preprocessing methods.

#### 13.3.2.1 Block-Based Non-local Means Algorithm

The traditional NLM algorithm may lead to poor results because of its nonlocality of neighboring pixels. To overcome this, a block-based NLM method is proposed, significantly reducing the computational time. The block-based NLM filter is more concrete in MRI and CT images since they are primarily 3D or stacks of 2D. Thus, in biomedical image denoising, computational efficiency is vital. To maintain global continuity, this work overlaps adjacent blocks by one column or row of pixels. The multiple approximations of the restored intensity value at the pixel xi are then averaged among several approximations. While dealing with large datasets, averaging intensity values produces high computational costs.

Therefore, rather than considering pixels, an enhanced NLM is suggested using blocks of size (2*α* + 1)² with overlapping constraints. Later, the NLM restoration is performed on these blocks rather than on pixels. The block-based enhanced NLM method is described by

(13.1)$NL\\left\\lbrack u \\right\\rbrack\\left( B\_{ik} \\right) = \\sum\\limits\_{B\_{j}\\epsilon\\ v\_{ik}}^{}w\\left( {B\_{ik},\\, B\_{j}} \\right)\\ u\\left( B\_{j} \\right)$ 

where

$w\\left( {B\_{ik,}\\ B\_{j,}} \\right) = \\left\\{ {\\frac{1}{Z\_{ik}}e^{- \\frac{\\parallel {u{(B\_{ik})} - u{(B\_{j})} \\parallel^{2}}}{\\widehat{h}}}\\ \\ 0} \\right.\\,\\,{otherwise\\; if}\\;\\mu\_{1} < \\frac{u\\left( \\underset{\\\_}{B\_{ik}} \\right)}{u\\left( B\_{j} \\right)} < \\frac{1}{\\mu\_{1}}\\;{and}\\;\\sigma\_{1}^{2} < \\frac{\\operatorname{var}\\left( {u\\left( B\_{ik} \\right)} \\right)}{\\operatorname{var}\\left( {u\\left( B\_{j} \\right)} \\right)} < \\frac{1}{\\sigma\_{1}^{2}}$ 

*Z[ik]* is a constant of normalization satisfying ∑[*B*[*j*]*ϵ* *v*[*i**k*]]*w*(*B*[*i**k*], *B*[*j*]) = 1 and *ĥ* is a parameter for smoothness. In addition, the most similar neighborhoods are selected well in advance to avoid unnecessary weight computation. The weight factors are computed only when the ratio of the mean and variance of *u*(*B[ik]*) and *u*(*B[j]*) are in the range of 1.

#### 13.3.2.2 Thresholding Using Median Filtering with Pixel Modeling (MF–PM) Technique in the Wavelet Domain

Initially, the wavelet transform is applied to the CT abdomen image. Then, the high-frequency subbands are denoised using adaptive thresholding with the Bayes shrinkage function. Finding the optimal threshold value is essential for preserving clinical details and noise suppression. This work obtains the threshold value using noise variance and the standard deviation of noise-free images. Let us consider that *α* is the threshold value, and it is given by

(13.2)$\\alpha = \\frac{\\sigma\_{\\vartheta}^{2}}{\\sigma\_{y}}$ 

where, α is the noise variance that is estimated by the robust median estimation method and it is given by

(13.3)${\\,\\sigma\\,}\_{\\vartheta}^{2} = \\left( \\frac{{median(}\\left| {x\\left( {m,n} \\right)} \\right|}{0.6475} \\right)^{\\! 2}$ 

*x(m,n)* ̴ *H[L]* represents the level in the wavelet domain. The standard deviation of the noise-free image is given by

(13.4)*σ* [*y*]² = *m**a**x*(*σ* [*x*]² − *σ* [*ϑ*]², 0 ) 

where

$\\sigma\_{x}^{2} = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{i\\! = \\! 1}^{N}X\_{i}^{2}$ and *N* represents an input image. Then the thresholding function is given by

(13.5)*X̂* = {0 *f*|*X*| ≤ *α* *s**i**g**n**u**m*(*x*)(|*X*| − *α**f*|*X*| > *α* 

The obtained results show that the preprocessing results of the proposed median filtering with pixel modeling (MF-PM) technique yield better performance when compared to other methods. The edge details are preserved in this method by considering the pixel array-based filtering technique. However, in the NLM technique, the factual edges vanish due to the significant value of the standard deviation of the Gaussian filter.

### 13.3.3 Deep Learning Model-Based Image Prediction

In this work, the cascaded encoder-decoder CNN (CEDCNN) method is engaged for effective liver segmentation and tumors from CT abdomen images. The CEDCNN structure is composed of an encoder and decoder network, which are symmetric, as shown in [Figure 13.4](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_fig_004). The proposed architecture resembles the SegNet model. In the conventional SegNet architecture, the first 14 convolutional layers are used by the encoder-network component of a traditional SegNet design. Because the encoder and decoder networks are symmetrical, the decoder network includes 13 convolutional layers. The softmax classifier function uses the decoder network output to generate a probability class for all pixels. Then, a convolution-based filter bank extracts the normalized feature map. In this work, the rectified linear nonlinearity (ReLU) unit is followed by batch normalization. Finally, the ReLU is subjected to max pooling with window size 2 × 2 and stride 2, followed by subsampling. The decoder network upsamples the input feature maps. A decoder filter bank creates the dense feature map by applying a convolution operator to the upsampling. Each of these feature maps is also subjected to batch normalization. The final stage of the decoder network yields a multichannel feature map that resembles an input image. The softmax classifier function uses this multichannel feature map to identify the pixels in the input image.

![Figure 13.4: General structure of cascaded encoder-decoder CNN (CEDCNN).](graphic/converted/b_9783111436180-013_fig_004.png)

Figure 13.4: General structure of cascaded encoder-decoder CNN (CEDCNN).

[Figure 13.5](#9783111436050_032892.xhtml#b_9783111436180-013_fig_005) illustrates the model used by the CEDCNN approach, which consists of 41 layers: 3 FC (fully connected) layers, 2 × 2 maxpooling, and 13 convolutional layers. SegNet, an encoder-decoder technique suggested by VGG-16, uses predefined weights. It has a classification layer based on pixels as well as an encoder-decoder network. Convolution and max pooling will occur at the encoder network since VGG-16 is the encoder portion, which has 13 convolutional layers. Additionally, a 2 × 2 max pooling is carried out, leading to the corresponding storage of indices. The decoder network maps using a resolution encoder and then provides the results to the classification layers.

![Figure 13.5: Basic block diagram of CEDCNN with VGG16 architecture.](graphic/converted/b_9783111436180-013_fig_005.png)

#### 13.3.3.1 Training

A random selection of 15 sets comprising 2,234 cuts was utilized for training, while the remaining five sets with 591 slices were used for testing in this study. Additionally, during the CEDCNN training, no data augmentation is utilized. During the training phase, the two-fold normalization approach is used for the CT image (I) and the related ground truth image (G). Finally, each CT image and ground truth image is divided into different slices with an image size of 256 × 256 before starting the training phase. The input is provided with the normalized 2D images and ground truth sets to fit a rough segmentation model. This model primarily distinguishes between liver and background characteristics.

On the other hand, any 3D volume must meet specific requirements. Each 3D volume must be resized to a voxel size of 1 mm³. Finally, the normalized images are cropped using the liver mask. A dense training approach is adopted to fit an acceptable liver segmentation model. The stochastic gradient descent method is used as an optimizer during training. The learning rate progressively reduces every 50 epochs from 0.1 to 0.00450, with a 0.4 drop factor. The network is trained for 150 epochs with a batch size of 8. The first CNN output is a binary representation of expected liver areas, which are then utilized as input to the CNN by extracting ROIs.

#### 13.3.3.2 Testing

The liver region will be segmented from abdominal images during the testing stage. As in the training stage, in the testing phase, two-fold image normalization is also done once the 3D testing images are normalized into 2D slices. Then, a coarse liver segmentation is predicted using the trained structure. Alternatively, the input CT and roughly segmented liver images are resized to a regularized voxel size. Finally, the trained 3D fully convolutional neural network produces fine and rough liver tumor segmentation.

#### 13.3.3.3 Performance Evaluation Metrics

The performance of the proposed preprocessing, liver segmentation, and tumor segmentation methods is analyzed based on the following measures.

#### 13.3.3.4 Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR)

The peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) is a performance indicator that measures how the mean square errors introduced into the original image throughout the filtering process compare to the square of the maximum pixel value. The PSNR is given as follows:

(13.6)${PSNR}\\left( {dB} \\right) = 10\\,{lo}g\_{10}\\frac{{ma}x^{2}}{MSE}$ 

where "max" indicates the maximum pixel value of the input image, and PSNR suggests the quality of the reconstructed image. The increased PSNR value results in the enhanced quality of the image.

#### 13.3.3.5 Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASD)

It calculates the surface distance based on the voxels of two segmentations by considering the average of all saved distances. The average value of all stored distances is zero, and this indicates perfect segmentation.

It is one of the most commonly used measures in terms of mm, as follows:

(13.7)$\\frac{{ASD}\\left( {mm} \\right) = {{\\sum\_{x\\epsilon X}{min}}\_{y\\epsilon Y}\\left( {d\\left( {x,y} \\right)} \\right) + \\sum\_{y\\epsilon Y}{min}\_{x\\epsilon X}\\left( {d\\left( {x,y} \\right)} \\right)}}{N\_{X} + N\_{Y}}$ 

where *X* and *Y* indicate the reference surface and segmented volume surface, *x* and *y* represent the mesh points of *X* and *Y*, *d*(*x*, *y*) indicates the distance between *x* and *y*, then *N[X]* and *N[Y]* are the number of points on *X* and *Y*, respectively.

#### 13.3.3.6 Root Mean-Squared Symmetric Surface Distance (RMSD)

It measures the surface difference between two different segmentations by considering the surface distance. It is required to square the surface voxels before storing them. It is premeditated as an equation in terms of mm:

(13.8) ${RMSD}\\left( {mm} \\right) = \\sqrt{\\frac{\\sum\_{x\\epsilon X}^{}\\min\_{y\\epsilon Y}\\left( {d\\left( {x,y} \\right)} \\right)^{2} + \\sum\_{y\\epsilon Y}^{}\\min\_{x\\epsilon X}\\left( {d\\left( {x,y} \\right)} \\right)^{2}}{N\_{X} + N\_{Y}}}$ 

#### 13.3.3.7 Maximum Symmetric Surface Distance (MSD)

It is a measure based on the Euclidean distance. It is defined as the difference between the surface voxels. Then, the maximum surface value provides the maximum MSD. It is calculated as in eq. (13.9):

(13.9)*M**S**D*(*m**m*) = max (max[*x**ϵ**X*](min[*y**ϵ**Y*](*d*(*x*,*y*))),max[*y**ϵ**Y*](*d*(*x*,*y*))) 

#### 13.3.3.8 Volumetric Overlap Error (VOE)

This metric measures the difference in volume between the reference image and the volume of the liver-segmented image. To measure this metric, the average of all slices is considered for measuring the metrics in terms of percentage of error. It is calculated as follows:

(13.10)${VOE}(\\%) = \\left( {1 - \\frac{V\_{seg} \\cap V\_{ref}}{V\_{seg} \\cup V\_{ref}}} \\right) \\times 100$ 

where *V*[seg] is the segmented image and *V*[ref] is the reference image. This method effectively shows the segmentation accuracy. If the volumetric overlap error is zero, it indicates segmentation accuracy.

#### 13.3.3.9 Signed Relative Volume Difference (SRVD)

It measures the volume difference between the segmented and input images. It is expressed in terms of percentage and is calculated as in eq. (13.11):

(13.11)${SRVD}\\left( \\% \\right) = \\frac{\\left| {v\_{seg} - v\_{ref}} \\right|}{v\_{ref}} \\times 100$ 

Based on these measures, the performance of the proposed techniques is evaluated. A smaller value in all evaluation metrics leads to a better segmentation result.

### 13.3.4 Tumor Classification Module

The main intention of the classification module is to differentiate the type of tumor present in the segmented tumor image. Classification of the tumor is the final stage in the CAD model. The difference in features extracted from the segmented liver tumor is given as input to the classifier stage in this stage. The essential task in the tumor classification stage is the extraction and selection of features. In this work, multilayer perceptron (MLP), support vector machine (SVM), and kappa statistics, random forest (RF) techniques are employed for classifying liver tumors.

In the existing work, the classification is done only by extracting the features from the lesion ROI. However, the novelty in this classification stage is considering two ROIs, which improves the accuracy by taking the difference of features extracted from the lesion and liver region. Initially, there are two types of ROI: one is a lesion (R1), and the other is surrounding normal liver tissue (R2). The features obtained using the first and second ROI will work as a novel feature vector. However, for identifying the normal liver tissue (R2), it is necessary to follow some constraints:

*   The ratio between the lesion ROI (R1) and the specific liver region (R2) is to be chosen as 1:1.7 by conducting several trials.
    
*   The typical liver region (R2) must centrally surround the lesion ROI (R1).
    
*   The lesion region (R1) is expelled from the typical liver region (R2).
    

In this manner, the features extracted from each of the tumor region and the surrounding region are considered to be a new feature vector.

## 13.4 Explainability Model

Model-agnostic interpretation techniques, which have recently been made possible by breakthroughs in ML, are used to explain complex models while maintaining good prediction performance. Separating the explanation model from the model-agnostic interpretation is more flexible than the model-specific explanation method. The two types of model-agnostic interpretation techniques are local explanation and global explanation. The most popular local explanation technique is local interpretable model-agnostic explanations(LIME). The two most common global interpretable techniques are PDP (partial dependence plots) and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations).

### 13.4.1 LIME Model

To provide interpretability for complicated models, LIME trains local surrogate models. LIME first produces a fresh dataset through data disruption. LIME then uses the new dataset to train an interpretable model, such as a decision tree. Finally, the black box model’s equivalent prediction performance is contrasted with the objective of the interpretable model. LIME is defined as follows:

(13.12)*γ*(*x*) = *a**r**g**m**i**n* *L*( *f*​, *g*, *Π*[*x*]) + *Ω*(*g*)*g**ϵ**G* 

where *L* is the loss function. The explainable model for instance *x* is represented by *g*. The interpretable model family is denoted as *G*. The closeness of the experimented instances to instance *x* is indicated by the instances *x*. *Ω* (*g*) defines the intricacy of model *g*.

### 13.4.2 PDP Model

PDP illustrates the small impact of a feature on the outcome predicted by a sophisticated ML model. It shows how the input and output are related to one another, whether it is more complicated, monotonous, or linear. The partial dependence function $\\widetilde{f\_{x\_{s}}}$ is given by the definition of

(13.13) $\\widetilde{f\_{x\_{s}}} = \\frac{1}{n}\\sum\\limits\_{i\\! = \\! 1}^{n}\\ \\widetilde{f\_{x\_{s}}}\\left( {x\_{s,}x\_{c}^{i}} \\right)$ 

where $\\widetilde{f\_{x\_{s}}}$ is the process that generates the overall relationship between an input feature and the expected result. The feature set “S” encompassing one or two features, *x[s]* denotes the set of features to be plotted $\\widetilde{f\_{x\_{s}}}$. *x[c]* designates the remaining features in the model, and *n* is the number of instances used in the dataset.

### 13.4.3 SHAP Model

It measures the impact of the feature on the multifaceted model with SHapley values. The sum of marginal aids is referred to as a SHapley value. It can be identified by the measure of closeness of prediction across all potential coalitions. The SHapley value is calculated by

(13.14)$\\varnothing\_{j}\\left( x \\right) = \\sum\\limits\_{s\\complement{\\{{x1,x2.\\ .\\ .,xm}\\}}{\\{ x\_{j}\\}}}^{}\\frac{\\left| s \\right|!\\left( {m - \\left| s \\right| - 1} \\right)!}{m!}\\left( {{val}\\left( {s \\cup \\left\\{ x\_{j} \\right\\} - {value}\\left( s \\right)} \\right)} \\right)$ 

where S is the SHapley value of *x[j]*, *x[j]* signifies a feature value, a feature subset of the model is represented by “*s*,” the number of features is denoted by *m*, and the value is the predicted feature values in set *s*.

Using K-fold cross-validation, the overall accuracy of the complex models was determined. *K* is typically set to 5, 10, or 20. ## 13.5 Conclusion

In this work, an explainable ML framework combines CEDCNN-based models with recently discovered explanation techniques to accurately predict the probability of liver diseases. The suggested framework is tested using public datasets from standard databases and nonpublic datasets collected from multidisciplinary scan centers. According to the results, the RF classifier method achieves the highest overall accuracy of 99.5% using a deep learning framework and an average accuracy of 95.4% using the XAI model with an RF-based classifier. The results of the proposed framework clarifications are reliable with the characteristics of liver tumors, which may help the radiologist to make more accurate diagnoses. In addition, this method promotes the application of AI in healthcare by highlighting the benefits of XAI frameworks in deciphering black-box models like RF. This work can be extended in the future by collecting more real-time liver images and investigating cutting-edge, model-independent techniques.

# 14 A Novel African Wild Dog Optimization (AWDO) Algorithm for Applications of Artificial Intelligence

Prabakaran Senthil Kumaran Shyamala 

#### Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI) harbors the potential to tackle intricate challenges and enhance human capabilities across various domains. Through its significant capabilities, AI plays a crucial role in data analysis, natural language processing (NLP), healthcare, and other decision-based fields. The primary objective of AI in these domains is to render precise decisions promptly. The attainment of higher decision-making accuracy and system performance enhancement necessitates the utilization of optimization algorithms to aid in the decision-making process efficiently. Swarm optimization draws inspiration from the collective behavior of animals or insects that cooperate in hunting, thereby facilitating rapid decision-making. This chapter delves into diverse swarm optimization algorithms that support decision-making processes in AI applications and introduces a novel algorithm called African wild dog optimization (AWDO). The proposed AWDO algorithm is an energy-efficient swarm optimization technique that minimizes energy consumption by AI nodes or neurons, resulting in expedited search outcomes. The efficacy of the AWDO algorithm is evaluated against established optimization algorithms like particle swarm optimization, ant colony optimization (ACO), artificial bee colony (ABC) optimization algorithm, firefly algorithm, and bacterial foraging optimization (BFO) algorithms in the realm of healthcare diagnosis applications.

Keywords:  Artificial intelligence,  African wild dog optimization,  particle swarm optimization,  ant colony optimization,  artificial bee colony,  firefly algorithm,  bacterial foraging optimization,  healthcare diagnosis,  

## 14.1 Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) \[[1](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_001)\] is an inevitably developing technology that creates the possibility for machines to learn from occurrences and make decisions on real-time events. The proliferation of AI has made it possible to make vital decisions and diagnoses in business and intelligence systems. Some of the vital applications of AI are market prediction, supply chain management, medical diagnosis, traffic analysis, image-based diagnosis, etc. Among the various applications, AI holds a major role in healthcare diagnosis systems, which involve cancer detection, early tumor detection, and many more related applications. Varieties of AI algorithms such as Naïve Bayes, support vector machine (SVM) \[[2](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_002)\], random forest (RF) \[[3](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_003)\], decision tree (DT) \[[4](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_004)\], neural networks (NN) \[[5](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_005)\], and deep learning (DL) algorithms \[[6](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_006)\] like convolutional neural networks (CNN) and recurrent neural networks (RNN) have been employed for the aforementioned applications.

Machine learning (ML) and the DL algorithm, which are subsets of the AI)technique, were applied for the diagnosis of multiple diseases from medical multimodal images. These multiple diseases include cancer, tumors, and other diseases at earlier stages. The medical image diagnosis is performed based on the dimension, region of interest (RoI), and the histogram \[[7](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_007)\] of the image pixel. The major challenge associated with AI-based medical image diagnosis is the feature selection process, as it often misses major and essential features for the classification process. Diseases like tumors necessitate the structural features of the tumor. The general structure of performing medical image diagnosis using an AI algorithm is depicted in [Figure 14.1](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_fig_001).

![Figure 14.1: General structure of medical image diagnosis using artificial intelligence.](graphic/converted/b_9783111436180-014_fig_001.png)

Figure 14.1: General structure of medical image diagnosis using artificial intelligence.

The computer-assisted diagnosis of human disease exhibits various advantages in terms of knowledge as well as accuracy in the classification process. However, the classification process is a complex one as it relies on various parameters. The most important aspect of the learning algorithms is the training of the model. The existing models were trained using the free datasets that were relevant to the particular type of human disease. Based on the volume of training data, the rate of accuracy of the diagnosis system \[[8](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_008)\] varies. In addition to the training data, the efficiency of the diagnosis model relies on the type of algorithm used for classification purposes. The algorithms of the DL model do not require any explicit input features, as they employ the features of the deep neural networks (DNN). The DNN employs multiple layers, namely “n” number of layers, for extracting the features from the input medical image. From the extracted features, the DNN model performs the feature selection process for efficient classification and diagnosis. Despite the advantages of DL in the medical image diagnosis process, it experiences major challenges of shortfall in terms of accuracy due to the feature selection process and the degradation of edges of the input images. This causes essential images to deteriorate in terms of efficiency and thus necessitates the requirement of advanced AI technology \[[9](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_009)\] for efficient and accurate medical image diagnosis. The existing methodologies fall short in terms of global search, impacting the accuracy in the diagnosis process. In addition, the optimization function \[[10](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_010)\] is trapped under the local optima, thus leading to weak characteristics in robustness to the local optima. The major objectives of the proposed work are to classify the medical images with an enhanced level of accuracy using the African wild dog optimization (AWDO) algorithm. The proposed method is highly robust in preserving the features of the input image. In addition to the increase in accuracy, the proposed work excels in terms of precision, recall, and biopsy rate. The organization of this chapter is structured with a basic introduction in Section 14.1, literature analysis in Section 14.2, and a detailed description of the proposed novel AWDO algorithm in Section 14.3. The case study is performed, and the analysis of the proposed work is presented in Section 14.4. The chapter is concluded with the highlights of the proposed work in Section 14.5.

## 14.2 Literature Review

The smart medication process followed over the past decade motivates numerous researchers to employ and introduce novel classification algorithms in diagnosing specific diseases in human beings. This section illustrates the notable research results of AI in terms of medical image diagnosis, such as tumor detection and cancer detection.

Jabbar et al. \[[11](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_011)\] proposed a Caps-VGGNet hybrid model \[[11](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_011)\] for the diagnosis of tumor detection. The authors employed the Brats dataset for training the model, and the major challenge of the introduced model is the requirement of a huge volume of data for training the model to achieve a high level of accuracy. Mo et al. \[[12](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_012)\] proposed a Hover-Trans block extraction model \[[12](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_012)\] to determine breast cancer at an earlier stage. The authors employed the GDPH dataset for training the model and used sonogram images for the detection process. Li et al. \[[13](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_013)\] developed a frequency-guided diffusion model \[[13](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_013)\] for processing and diagnosing medical images. The proposed model is capable of diagnosing any type of medical disease, provided the system is fed with the appropriate training datasets. Wu et al. \[[14](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_014)\] introduced a nonlocal algorithm \[[14](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_014)\] based on AI techniques to detect anomalies in human MRI images. The proposed model is highly robust and optimized the boundaries of the input image.

Asiri et al. \[[15](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_015)\] introduced a dual computerized model \[[15](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_015)\] for enhancing the accuracy of the diagnosis of input medical images. The first model aims at the image enhancement process using neural networks and the principal component analysis method. The latter model employs the support vector machine for performing the classification of the input tumor image. The classification is performed after the segmentation process and achieved an accuracy of 89.9%. Shamsad et al. (2024) contributed to early medical image diagnosis by designing an AI-based transfer learning model \[[16](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_016)\]. The proposed model aimed to enhance the accuracy in detecting anomalies in input medical images. The authors employed VGG-16 and VGG-19 datasets for training and testing the proposed model.

Palkar et al. \[[17](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_017)\] designed a Glioma prognosis model \[[17](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_017)\] using the AI technique. The proposed work was compared with existing AI models like random forest, support vector machine, CatBoost, LGBM classifier, and XGBoost to prove its supremacy in terms of accuracy in classifying the input medical image. Asif et al. \[[18](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_018)\] employed AI tools \[[18](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_018)\] for analyzing biomedical datasets in diagnosing medical images at the early stages. The authors employed ML and DL models for the diagnosis of HCC images.

Prakash et al. \[[19](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_019)\] presented an advanced framework for the medical image diagnosis process using the generative adversarial network (GAN) model \[19\]. The proposed GAN model is a three-dimensional model that accepts CT images of the kidney to detect and predict the presence of tumors in the kidney. The authors employed a structural GAN model to produce a minimum of 20% enhancement in the accuracy of the prediction process. Siddique et al. \[[20](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_020)\] introduced an innovative training model using the Inception V3 model \[[20](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_020)\] and employed the particle swarm optimization algorithm for detecting and classifying anomalies in tumors in various parts of the human body. The authors employed the INCEPT training model and achieved an accuracy of 90.5%.

The major drawbacks of the existing AI-based medical image diagnosis model are as follows.

*   The existing classification model employs excessive classification parameters, leading to an increase in the complexity of the model.
    
*   The rate of convergence of the existing models is very slow, and the optimization rate is considerably low.
    
*   The robustness of the existing works was low, and it feels hard to diagnose the noisy input medical images.
    
*   Due to the decrease in the level of robustness, the level of accuracy also sheds to a greater extent.
    

To overcome the above-mentioned challenges of the existing classification methods, the AWDO is employed to achieve the following contributions in the medical image diagnosis process.

*   The proposed AWDO classification algorithm is highly robust and will accept noisy input medical images for the classification process.
    
*   The proposed AWDO algorithm accepts minimal parameters, which possess the least complexity in terms of the classification process.
    
*   The proposed AWDO is a promising optimization technique with the potential to provide efficient and effective solutions to a wide range of challenging problems.
    

## 14.3 Proposed Model

The proposed AWDO is a metaheuristic algorithm designed based on the inspiration of the hunting behavior of African dogs. This intelligent algorithm demonstrates the team work efforts of the African dogs, its adaptability, and its efficiency in hunting its prey. A similar pattern is employed in the proposed work to determine the anomalous behavior of the input medical image. In this proposed scheme of the optimization process, the swarm of African dogs, namely 5–20 dogs, is directed by the pair of leader dogs as depicted in [Figure 14.2](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_fig_002). The leader dogs organize the member dogs and act as the best pairs of dogs in the hunting process. The leader dog pairs perform decision-making processes, controlling the member dogs, and hunting and resting processes. Inspired by this hunting behavior, the proposed AWDO algorithm identifies the anomalous behavior or pattern of the input medical image by employing a pair of threshold pixels, namely threshold pixel-row wise (*P[R]*) and threshold pixel-column wise (*P[C]*). Based on the threshold pixels, the comparative process is performed with the remaining pixels to determine the anomalous pattern in the input medical image.

![Figure 14.2: Hunting behavior of African wild dogs.](graphic/converted/b_9783111436180-014_fig_002.png)

Figure 14.2: Hunting behavior of African wild dogs.

The threshold pixels *P[R]* and *P[C]* are responsible for determining the anomaly pattern among the input image pixels by determining the difference among the pixel values. It is notable that the threshold pixels *P[R]* and *P[C]* are not permanent, and the pair shall be modified based on the search. The major activities of the threshold pixels *P[R]* and *P[C]* are determining the anomaly pattern pixels, reviewing the anomaly pixels, selecting the surrounding pixels of the anomaly pixels, and classification of the pixels. The basic architecture of the proposed AWDO-based medical image diagnosis is presented in [Figure 14.3](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_fig_003).

![Figure 14.3: Architecture of the proposed AWDO-based medical image diagnosis.](graphic/converted/b_9783111436180-014_fig_003.png)

Figure 14.3: Architecture of the proposed AWDO-based medical image diagnosis.

The mathematical models for the pixel analysis for the anomaly behavior, tracking, and the classification process are presented in this section. The parent threshold pixels *P[R]* and *P[C]* are supported by the other pairs of pixels at various levels, namely different rows and columns. The pixel identification process, determined by the threshold pixels *P[R]* and *P[C]*[,] is defined as follows:

(14.1)*P*[*r*](*n*) = |*P*[*T**R*](*n*)−*α*×*P*[*t**R*](*n*)|*P⃗*(*t*) − *D⃗*(*t*) (14.2)               *P*[*C*](*n*) = |*P*[*T**C*](*n*)−*β*×*P*[*t**C*](*n*)|*P⃗*(*t*+1) − *D⃗*(*t*+1) 

[Equations (14.1](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_eq_001)) and (14.2) represent the target pixels in terms of rows and columns along with the vectors *P⃗*(*t*) *a**n**d* *D⃗*(*t*). The vectors *P⃗*(*t*) *a**n**d* *D⃗*(*t*) shall be determined using [eqs. (14.3](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_eq_003)) and (14.[4](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_eq_004)), respectively.

(14.3)$\\overrightarrow{P}\\left( t \\right) = \\overset{\\rightarrow}{r\_{1}}\\left( t \\right) - 2.\\alpha\\overset{\\rightarrow}{r\_{2}}\\left( t \\right)$ (14.4)$\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\overrightarrow{D}\\left( t \\right) = \\overset{\\rightarrow}{r\_{3}}\\left( {t + 1} \\right) - 2.\\beta\\overset{\\rightarrow}{r\_{4}}\\left( {t + 1} \\right)$ 

During the process of iteration, the vectors *α* and *β* are chosen randomly in the range of 0 to 1. The terms *r*[1], *r*[2], *r*[3,] and *r*[4] are random vectors chosen at random in the range of pixels (0-m) rows and (0-n) columns. The threshold wild dogs (pixels) coordinates in the pixel position (*m,n*) are used to update the new position of the anomaly pixels in the input medical image. The location of the wild dogs shall be adjusted with the factors *α* and *β* in the input medical image. The new locations of the wild dogs in determining the anomaly pattern are represented in [eqs. (14.5](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_eq_005))–(14.10), respectively.

(14.5)*P⃗*[*A*](*t*) = |*P⃗*(*t*)−*D⃗*(*t*)| × |*P⃗*(*t*−1)−*D⃗*(*t*−1)| × |*P⃗*(*t*+1)−*D⃗*(*t*+1)| (14.6)*P⃗*[*A*1](*t*) = |*P⃗*(*t*)−*D⃗*(*t*)| × *α*[1]*β*[1] (14.7)*P⃗*[*A*2](*t*) = |*P⃗*(*t*−1)−*D⃗*(*t*−1)| × *α*[2]*β*[2] (14.8)*P⃗*[*A*3](*t*) = |*P⃗*(*t*+1)−*D⃗*(*t*+1)| × *α*[3]*β*[3] (14.9) *P⃗*[*A*4](*t*) = |*P⃗*(*t*−*m*)−*D⃗*(*t*−*n*)| × *α*[4]*β*[4] (14.10)*P⃗*[*A*5](*t*) = |*P⃗*(*t*+*m*)−*D⃗*(*t*+*n*)| × *α*[5]*β*[5] 

The *P⃗*[*A*](*t*) is the target anomaly pixel, whereas the *P⃗*[*A*1](*t*) to *P⃗*[*A*5](*t*) is surrounding wild dog pixels are located by the parent threshold pair of the pixels to classify the anomaly pixel. The members of the WDO support the searching process for the anomaly pattern in the input medical image. The vectors *P⃗*(*t*) *a**n**d* *D⃗*(*t*) are the pairs of hunting dogs that help in attacking the anomaly pixel of the input medical image. The proposed work intentionally employs the two vectors to emphasize exploration and performs the iteration process to determine the anomaly pattern. The movement of the patterns is performed using the two constants, namely *α* and *β*, respectively. The targeted pixel undergoes a classification process to determine whether the pixel is infected or normal using the conditional [equations (14.11](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_eq_011)) and (14.[12](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_eq_012)), respectively:

(14.11)*I**f* *P⃗*[*A*](*t*) ≥ *P⃗*[*T*](*t*) (14.12)*I**f* *P⃗*[*A*](*t*) < *P⃗*[*T*](*t*) 

If the pixel value of the target pixel is greater than the pixel value of the threshold pixel, then it is classified as an infected pixel. Otherwise, as represented in [eq. (14.12](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_eq_012)), it is classified as a normal pixel. The AWDO algorithm for performing medical image diagnosis is presented in [Table 14.1](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_tab_001).

## 14.4 Comparative Analysis

The proposed AWDO for determining anomalies in the input multi-modal medical images is analyzed against accuracy, precision, recall, and *F*1 score, and compared with the performance of state-of-the-art methodologies. The performance of the proposed work is compared with state-of-the-art algorithms like support vector machine \[[21](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_021)\], random forest \[[22](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_022)\], decision tree \[[23](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_023)\], particle swarm optimization \[[24](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_024)\], K-means clustering \[[25](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_025)\], DNN \[[26](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_026)\], and recurrent neural networks \[[27](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_027)\]. The model is trained with the BRATS dataset containing brain tumor images and is tested with images from the same dataset.

The term "accuracy" in terms of medical image diagnostics is considered a critical parameter that assists in determining further treatment. The accuracy is influenced by various parameters like the quality of the input image, tumor heterogeneity, availability of the data, complexity of the algorithm, feature extraction process, and preprocessing algorithm, along with its effectiveness in removing noise from the input test image. The accuracy of the classification is determined in terms of a confusion matrix with true positive (TP), true negative (TN), false positive (FP), and false negative (FN), as depicted in [Figure 14.4](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_fig_004).

![Figure 14.4: Confusion matrix for medical image prediction.](graphic/converted/b_9783111436180-014_fig_004.png)

Figure 14.4: Confusion matrix for medical image prediction.

The mathematical representation of the accuracy in terms of the confusion matrix is defined as follows:

(14.17)${Accuracy}\\left( A \\right) = \\frac{TP\\, + \\, TN}{TP\\, + \\, TN\\, + \\, FP\\, + \\, FN}$ 

Precision is the performance metric employed to evaluate the quality of the positive predictions made by the proposed classification model. Specifically, precision is the rate at which predictions were made correctly by the classification model. The mathematical representation of precision is defined as follows:

(14.18) ${Precision}\\left( P \\right) = \\frac{TP}{TP\\, + \\, FP}$ 

A high precision performance of the classification model indicates that the model is likely to be correct in terms of the classification process. Recall is the alternative parameter for precision, which could be defined as the metric used for determining the actual positive cases that were correctly identified. The term recall can also be termed as sensitivity and is mathematically represented as follows:

(14.19)${Recall}\\left( R \\right) = \\frac{TP}{TP\\, + \\, FN}$ 

The recall parameter determines the proportion of actual positive cases that were correctly predicted. The term *F*1 score is the integrated metric of recall and precision to form a single rate of classification. The *F*1 score is usually determined to identify the balance between the precision and recall of the classification model. The mathematical representation of the *F*1 score is defined as follows:

(14.20)$F1\\ \\,{score\\, = \\,}\\frac{{2\\, \\times \\,}\\left( {{Precision\\, \\times \\,}\\,{Recall}} \\right)}{\\left( {{Precision}\\,{\\, + \\,}\\,{Recall}} \\right)}$ 

The observed values of the above-mentioned parameters by the state-of-the-art methodologies like support vector machine \[[21](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_021)\], random forest \[[22](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_022)\], decision tree \[[23](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_023)\], particle swarm optimization \[[24](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_024)\], K-means clustering \[[25](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_025)\], DNN \[[26](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_026)\], and recurrent neural networks \[[27](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_027)\] are listed in [Table 14.2](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_tab_002).

The proposed model of the AWDO classification algorithm is known for its reduced complexity in terms of performance. In this context, the computational time \[[29](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_ref_029)\] is measured in the proposed work by providing various types of medical MRI images. Various input images were fed to the proposed model, and the results are depicted in [Table 14.3](#9783111436050_037035.xhtml#b_9783111436180-014_tab_003).

The performance analysis proves that the proposed AWDO work demonstrates its supremacy in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, and *F*1 score in diagnosing the medical MRI image, along with reduced computational time.

## 14.5 Conclusion

Medical image diagnosis is a major thrust area and necessitates the incorporation of technology for accurate predictions. Various technologies have been involved in the classification of tumors in various parts of the body and cancer cells, but still experience a major setback in terms of accuracy and consume an enhanced level of computational time. This proposed work employs the AWDO model, which accepts noisy input images and consumes reduced computational time when compared with state-of-the-art methodologies. The AWDO model is designed based on the behavior of the hunting technique employed by African wild dogs. The performance of the proposed AWDO model is compared with existing methodologies, and the results prove that the proposed AWDO model stands ahead in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, and *F*1 score. In addition, the proposed AWDO model consumes reduced computational complexity. The performance of the proposed AWDO model can further be enhanced with the incorporation of fuzzy logic and rules along with the AWDO model.

# 15 Artificial Intelligence-Based Control Strategies for COVID-19 That Target Different Age Groups

S. Saranya 

#### Abstract

This chapter describes artificial intelligence (AI) tools in the mathematical model of COVID-19 disease with medication and various methods to control its spread. The age-structured populations’ general MC Kendrick equations are examined to create the model equations utilizing AI approaches to improve the precision and utility of a prey–predator system that pairs one predator with three age groups of prey. AI is useful for accounting for intricate interactions between predators and prey as well as for parameter estimation. We study the equilibria’s existence, positiveness, boundedness, and stability in relation to the inherent carrying capacity of the prey. The primary outcome of this study is the population’s distribution across three age groups and how to prevent disease transmission from predators by using both local and Hopf bifurcation methods. AI models the effects of various public health initiatives like lockdown and social distancing measures to control the spread of the virus. Lastly, the model’s output included numerical examples of Rossler-type AI tools in Maple software.

Keywords:  Point of equilibrium,  age group targets,  Hopf bifurcation, mathematical model of stability switch,  

## 15.1 Introduction

Many of the ideas and principles of the science being discussed are best communicated through mathematical models \[[17](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_017)\]. With the use of artificial intelligence (AI) approaches, predator–prey relations and rivalry are frequently seen as the two primary obstacles in population models based on mathematics \[[13](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_013), [18](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_018)\]. The behavior of predators and prey can be simulated mathematically to create more accurate predation models. Understanding and modeling the impact of their phenotypic traits require studying how predators and prey respond. Since these models rely heavily on empirical knowledge, they must be compared with the test results gathered in the virtual environment with the individuals present.

The COVID-19 pandemic was first identified in China and rapidly spread to the remainder of the world, leading the World Health Organization to proclaim a worldwide public health emergency. The third respiratory disease outbreak linked to the corona virus in the last 20 years is COVID-19, following Middle East respiratory syndrome and severe acute respiratory syndrome. COVID-19 has devastated the global healthcare system, resulting in thousands of deaths when it first surfaced in Wuhan, China. In the fight against the COVID-19 pandemic, it is critical to identify and screen affected persons as soon as possible because failure to do so could result in the spreading of virus to other people \[[20](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_020)\]. The actual COVID-19 data is a sequence of observations organized over time, and time-series prediction techniques are well-established in the statistics domain and include structure-based approaches, meta-predictors, and machine learning-based approaches \[[16](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_016)\].

Data is a fundamental prerequisite for building a framework that the AI community needs to handle this issue. The lack of appropriate data about patients infected with COVID-19 makes it difficult to create identification and analysis models \[[11](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_011)\]. Due to reluctance among patients to seek medical attention in order to avoid potential confinement, very little information is known about the COVID-19 test-positive patients. Furthermore, some infected individuals do not exhibit any COVID-19 symptoms, making it difficult to pinpoint the exact number of positive cases in large populations \[[14](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_014)\]. An infected individual becomes more dangerous for others the longer it takes to diagnose them. For this reason, the analysis depends heavily on the availability of vast amounts of data.

Numerous publications examining the impacts of COVID-19 from a statistical, mathematical, and computational standpoint have been released. Susceptible–infectious–recovered is one of the computational frameworks for examining the dynamics of COVID-19 virus. It calculates the spread of an epidemic by taking advantage of a time-dependent system of differential equations \[[11](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_011)\]. A thorough analysis of the research on predator–prey interactions conducted over the past century reveals how crucial this environment is to understand animal biology’s evolutionary and adaptive processes \[[18](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_018)\]. Providing for human needs and luxuries continuously depletes the natural world’s ecological balance \[[3](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_003), 7\]. The similar underlying methodology based on the aging group population has been utilized in mathematical models to describe the dynamics of diseases \[[19](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_019), [21](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_021)\]. Cushing inquired about numerous formulas for age-structured populations that were obtained from the Mc Kendrick model \[[15](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_015)\].

After highlighting the three distinct age groups of prey, we can say that:

1.  The age range of the first prey population is from birth to 14 years.
    
2.  Age range of the second prey population is 15–39 years.
    
3.  The third age group of prey is those over 40.
    

Due to their high degree of immunity and implementation of corrective measures, the first and second prey populations will experience a lower incidence of sickness. For the third prey population, which is 40 years of age and over, getting enough nutrients is essential for lowering the danger and severity of viral infections as well as strengthening the defense mechanism. The constant *τ* is interpreted as a gain in immunity, either through complementary medicine or government-provided vaccinations. In this study, we examine an AI model that simulates the dependence of temporal control measures (facial mask, elbow cough, hand washing, social distancing, and self-quarantine), based on the theory that people infected with COVID-19 can also carelessly transfer the illness \[[2](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_002)\].

![Figure 15.1: Control measures for corona virus.](graphic/converted/b_9783111436180-015_fig_001.png)

Figure 15.1: Control measures for corona virus.

Our primary objectives are: We investigate the optimal performance of AI techniques under the supposition that the control measures (social distancing, face masks, hand washing, elbow coughing, and self-quarantine) limit the infection and the spread of illness. We refer to the continual *τ* as a natural medicine or vaccination to increase the immune level of prey population, which is people under 40 years old. Distinct prey models are being created, representing distinct physical interactions between prey and predator species, derived from Lotka and Volterra’s groundbreaking work \[[12](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_012), [11](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_011)\]. Here, we are utilizing the carrying capacity for each of the three preys and the control mechanisms for the third prey \[[3](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_003)\]. We examine the Hopf bifurcation’s direction and stability as it arises at the boundary equilibrium point \[[9](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_009), [14](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_014)\].

This study retrieves the system and solves the guidelines for the system’s local stability \[[8](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_008)\]. Maintaining the balance of sickness in the prey–predator system is a crucial aspect of the ecosystem for natural coexistence and stability \[[5](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_005), 6\]. The results of our investigation into how three preys interact with a single predator model under varying incidences and disease-related mortality rates including vaccination and natural medicine are highlighted \[[2](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_002), [16](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_016)\]. Lastly, we display the numerical solution findings for every model at different parameter values. Symbolic computation and algebra, machine learning integration, natural language processing, predictive analysis, and other AI technologies are used in Maple 15 programming.

## 15.2 Technique for Choosing Values for Parameters

Three prey population subpopulations, shown by three prey populations, are created by the model from the whole population as *N*[1](*t*), *N*[2](*t*), *N*[3](*t*) at time *t*, and one predator population *N*[4](*t*). Examine the 4D model system as follows:

$\\ \\frac{dN\_{1}}{dt} = aN\_{1}\\left( {1 - \\frac{N\_{1}\\ }{k\_{1}}} \\right) - \\alpha\\ N\_{1}N\_{4}$ $\\ \\frac{dN\_{2}}{dt} = bN\_{2}\\left( {1 - \\frac{N\_{2}\\ }{k\_{2}}} \\right) - \\beta\\ N\_{2}N\_{4}$ $\\ \\frac{dN\_{3}}{dt} = cN\_{3}\\left( {1 - \\frac{N\_{3}\\ }{k\_{3}}} \\right) - \\gamma\\ N\_{3}N\_{4} - eN\_{3} + U\\tau N\_{3}$ (15.1)$\\ \\frac{dN\_{4}}{dt} = \\eta\\ N\_{1}N\_{4} + \\delta\\ N\_{2}N\_{4} + \\mu\\ N\_{3}N\_{4} - f\\,{\\! N\_{4}}$ 

with initial conditions

(15.2)*N*[*l*](*t*) ≥ 0, *N*[2](*t*) ≥ 0, *N*[3](*t*) ≥ 0, *N*[4](*t*) ≥ 0 

The first, second, third, and predator are denoted by the parameters *N*[1](*t*), *N*[2](*t*), *N*[3](*t*), and *N*[4](*t*), respectively, and may be found in this case. Here is a description of the model parameters:

The first, second, and third prey’s respective specific growth rates are **a, b, c.**

The corresponding carrying capabilities of the first, second, and third preys are *k*[1], *k*[2], *k*[3].

The predator interacts with three preys (*N*[1], *N*[2], *N*[3]) in the following ways: **α**, **β**, and **γ**.

**e** is the third prey population’s natural death. **U** represents the control shown in [Figure 15.1](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_fig_001). **τ** denotes the increased immunity with the intake of natural medicines.

The conversion factors for predators from the three prey populations are **η**, **δ**, and **μ**.

The natural death of the predator is *f*.

This model includes certain assumptions, consisting of:

1.  In the first, second, and third prey populations, interactions occur through predators.
    
2.  Strong immune growth from infancy to 39 years allows the first and second prey populations to recover after interactions with predators.
    
3.  Three populations of prey possessing carrying capacities and intrinsic growth rates of a, b, and c and *k*[1,] *k*[2], *k*[3 ] were fitted using the Leslie–Gower model, and no interaction was found between them.
    
4.  The virus only affects one-third of the prey population, as immunity develops and dies naturally. Also, we raise the immunity growth by AI through parameter estimation, such as constants *Uτ*, where *U* is the control measure (see Figure 4.1) and *τ* is the immunization or alternative medicine:
    
    *τ* = cardamom, ginger, turmeric, cumin seeds, and pepper
    
5.  After implementing control measures like *Uτ*, the afflicted prey recovers in a third prey population as a result of higher immune growth.
    
6.  Predators are weakened in primary and secondary prey populations, but not in tertiary prey populations.
    

## 15.3 Boundedness and Positivity of the Specified System

### 15.3.1 Positivity

**Theorem 15.1:** The given equation system (1) is never negative. Therefore, every potential outcome for system (15.1) is positive.

*Proof.*

Given that system (15.1)’s right-hand side is locally Lipschitzian on *C* and entirely continuous, condition (15.2) is distinct on \[0, *ξ*), where 0 < *ξ* ≤ +∞ as in \[[16](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_016)\]. With initial conditions (15.2) applied to system (15.1), we have

$N\_{1}\\left( t \\right) = N\_{1}\\left( 0 \\right)\\exp\\left\\lbrack {\\int\\left\\{ {a\\left( {1 - \\!\\frac{N\_{1}\\left( t \\right)}{k\_{1}}} \\right) - \\alpha N\_{4}\\left( t \\right)} \\right\\} dt} \\right\\rbrack\\! > {}0$ $N\_{2}\\left( t \\right) = N\_{2}\\left( 0 \\right)\\exp\\left\\lbrack {\\int\\left\\{ {b\\left( {1 - \\!\\frac{N\_{2}\\left( t \\right)}{k\_{2}}} \\right) - \\beta N\_{4}\\left( t \\right)} \\right\\} dt} \\right\\rbrack\\! > {}0$ $N\_{3}\\left( t \\right) = N\_{3}\\left( 0 \\right)\\exp\\left\\lbrack {\\int\\left\\{ {c\\left( {1 - \\!\\frac{N\_{3}\\left( t \\right)}{k\_{3}}} \\right) - \\gamma N\_{4}\\left( t \\right) + U\\tau} \\right\\} dt} \\right\\rbrack\\! > {}0$ *N*[4](*t*) = *N*[4](0)exp \[∫{*η**N*[1](*t*)+*δ**N*[2](*t*)+*μ**N*[3](*t*)−*f*}*d**t*\]​ > 0 

which brings the proof to an end.

### 15.3.2 Boundedness

**Theorem 15.2:** The domain contains bounds for the trajectories of system (15.1).

*R*[+]⁴ = {(*N*[*l*],*N*[2],*N*[3], *N*[4])∈*R*[+]⁴: *N*[*l*]≥0, *N*[2]≥0, *N*[3]≥0, *N*[4]≥*o*}.

*Proof.*

*D**e**f**i**n**e* *t**h**e* *f**u**n**c**t**i**o**n* *Δ* = *N*[*l*] + *N*[2] + *N*[3] + *N*[4] Take its temporal derivative with respect to solution (15.1):

$\\frac{dN}{dt} = \\frac{d\\ N\_{l}}{dt} + \\frac{d\\ N\_{2}}{dt} + \\frac{d\\ N\_{3}}{dt} + \\frac{d\\ N\_{4}}{dt}$

Since the solutions starting in *R*[+]⁴ continue in the non-negative quadrant and the parameters are non-negative, $\\ \\frac{\\ dN}{dt} + \\rho N = aN\_{1}\\left( {1 - \\frac{N\_{1}\\ }{k\_{1}}} \\right) + bN\_{2}\\left( {1 - \\frac{N\_{2}\\ }{k\_{2}}} \\right) + cN\_{3}\\left( {1 - \\frac{N\_{3}\\ }{k\_{3}}} \\right) - eN\_{3} + U\\tau N\_{3} - \\ fN\_{4} + \\rho N\_{1} + \\rho N\_{2} + \\rho N\_{3} + \\rho N\_{4}$

$= \\left( {\\rho + a} \\right)N\_{l} + \\left( {\\rho + b} \\right)N\_{2} + \\frac{\\left( {\\rho + c + U\\tau} \\right)\\ }{e}N\_{3} + \\left( {\\rho - f} \\right)N\_{4} - \\frac{aN\_{1}^{2}\\ }{k\_{1}} - \\frac{bN\_{2}^{2}\\ }{k\_{2}} - \\frac{cN\_{3}^{2}\\ }{k\_{3}}$

where *ρ* is an increasing constant for *ρ* > *f* and given *ϵ* > 0 exist to the extent that *t* on *t*  ≥  *t*[0]

$\\frac{dN}{dt} + \\rho N \\leq m + \\epsilon,m = \\min\\left\\{ {\\left( {\\rho + a} \\right),\\left( {\\rho + b} \\right),{\\frac{\\left( {\\rho + c + U\\tau} \\right)}{e},\\left( {\\rho - f} \\right)}} \\right\\}$

### 15.4.2 Analysis of Stability and Existence of Equilibrium Points

The existence and stability behavior of system (15.1) at the equilibrium locations are examined in this section \[[10](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_ref_010)\]:

*   The trivial equilibrium point *E*1 is a saddle point.
    
*   The axial equilibrium points *E*3 and *E*5 are saddle points.
    
*   The planar equilibrium points *E*4 and *E*6 are saddle points.
    
*   The planar equilibrium of *E*2, *E*11, *E*13, and *E*14 is unstable.
    
*   The planar equilibrium of *E*7, *E*8, *E*9, *E*10, and *E*12 are asymptotically stable locally. The equilibrium points *E*7, *E*8, *E*9, *E*10, *E*12, and the internal equilibrium point *E*15 will be interpreted.
    
*   At equilibrium, the Jacobian matrix of system (15.1) will interpret the equilibrium points *E*7, *E*8, *E*9, *E*10, *E*12, and the interior equilibrium point *E*15.
    

System (15.1)’s equilibrium point Jacobian matrix *E* = (*N*[1](*t*),*N*[2](*t*),*N*[3](*t*),*N*[4](*t*)) is given by

*J* = \[*m*[11] 0 0−*N*[1]*α* 0 *m*[22] 0−*N*[2]*β* *o* 0 *m*[33]−*N*[3]*γ* *N*[4]*η* *N*[4]*δ* *N*[4]*μ* *m*[44]\] 

where $m\_{11} = a - 2\\frac{a\\ N\_{1}\\ }{\\ k\_{1}} - N\_{4}\\alpha,\\ m\_{22} = b - 2\\frac{b\\ N\_{2}\\ }{\\ k\_{2}} - N\_{4}\\beta,\\ m\_{33} = c - 2\\frac{c\\ N\_{3}\\ }{\\ k\_{3}} - N\_{4}\\gamma - e + U\\tau$, *m*[44] = *N*[1]*η* + *N*[2]*δ* + *N*[3]*μ* − *f*.

Due to the nature of the eigenvalues, eq. (15.1) is stable if all eigenvalues are negative for the real roots of the Jacobian characteristic equation above, and have negative real parts for the complex roots. Otherwise, the system will become unstable.

where *M*3 = 4*I* − (*m*11+*m*22+*m*33+*m*44) = 4*I* − *X*

$\\begin{matrix} {M2 = \\, 6I^{2}} & {- (m11 + m22 + m33 + m44)3I + m22m33 + m22m44 + m33m44 + m11m22} \\\\ & {+ m11m33 + m11m44 - N\_{3}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\mu\\gamma + N\_{1}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\eta\\alpha} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$  = 6*I*² − 3*X**I* + (*Y* + *j*[1]) $\\begin{matrix} & {M1 = 4I^{3} - (m11 + m22 + m33 + m44)3I^{2} + (2m22m33 + 2m22m44 +} \\\\ & {2m33m44 + 2m22m11 + 2m33m11 + 2m44m11 + 2N\_{3}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\gamma\\mu + 2N\_{1}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\alpha\\eta + N\_{2}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\delta\\beta)I -} \\\\ & {m22m33m44 - m22m33m11 - m22m44m11 - m33m44m11 - N\_{3}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\gamma\\mu m22 -} \\\\ & {N\_{3}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\gamma\\mu m11 - N\_{2}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\delta\\beta m11 - N\_{1}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\alpha\\eta m22 - N\_{1}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\alpha\\eta m33} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$  = 4*I*³ − 3*X**I*² + (2(*Y*+*j*[1])+*j*[2])*I* − *Z* $\\begin{matrix} & {M0 = I^{4} - (m11 + m22 + m33 + m44)I^{3} + (m11m22 + m11m33 + m11m44 +} \\\\ & {m22m33 + m33m44 + m22m44 - N\_{3}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\gamma\\mu - N\_{2}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\delta\\beta - N\_{1}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\alpha\\eta)I^{2} - (m11m22m33 +} \\\\ & {m11m22m44 + m11m33m44 + m22m33m44 + m11N\_{3}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\gamma\\mu +} \\\\ & {N\_{3}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\gamma\\mu m22 + N\_{2}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\delta\\beta m33 + N\_{2}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\delta\\beta m11 + N\_{1}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\alpha\\eta m22 + N\_{1}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\alpha\\eta m33)I +} \\\\ & {m11m22m33m44 - m11\\, N\_{3}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\gamma\\mu m22 + N\_{2}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\delta\\beta m11m33 + N\_{1}^{\\ast}N\_{4}^{\\ast}\\alpha\\eta m33m22} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$  = *I*⁴ − *X**I*³ + (*Y*−*j*[1]+*j*[2])*I*² − (*Z*+*j*[3]) + *W*

## 15.5 Hopf bifurcation

The Hopf bifurcation around the interior equilibrium point *E*15 was studied in this section. The bifurcation parameter *N*[3] is identified by the basic parameter *c*, which represents the prey’s growth rate. The Jacobian matrix *J*[*E*15] experiences Hopf bifurcation, wherein two of its eigenvalues are solely imaginary, while the remaining eigenvalues containing non-positive real components are  *R**e*\[*d**λ*/*d**c*\]|[*c* = *c*[0]] ≠ 0\[4\]. Assume that the interior equilibrium point’s characteristic equation *E*15 is as follows:

(15.3)*λ*⁴ + *A*[3]*λ*³ + *A*[2]*λ*² + *A*[1]*λ*¹ + *A*[0] = 0 

The characteristic polynomial coefficients (15.3) meet the following requirement for just imaginary eigenvalues *A*3*A*2*A*1 − *A*[3]²*A*0 − *A*[1]² = 0.

Assume that ±*iω* represents two purely imaginary eigenvalues that match c0. From the characteristic equation (15.3),

$\\left\\lbrack {4\\lambda^{3} + 3A\_{3}\\lambda^{2} + 2A\_{2}\\lambda + A\_{1}} \\right\\rbrack\\ \\frac{d\\lambda}{dc} + \\left( {\\lambda^{3}\\frac{dA}{dc} + \\lambda^{2}\\frac{dA}{dc} + \\lambda\\frac{dA}{dc} + \\frac{dA}{dc}} \\right) = 0$ 

Hence

(15.4)$\\frac{d\\lambda}{dc} = \\! - \\!\\left( \\frac{\\lambda^{3}\\ \\frac{dA}{dc} + \\lambda^{2}\\ \\frac{dA}{dc} + \\lambda\\ \\frac{dA}{dc} + \\frac{dA}{dc}}{4\\lambda^{3} + 3A\_{3}\\lambda^{2} + 2A\_{2}\\lambda + A\_{1}} \\right)$ 

When we change *iω* in [eq. (15.4)](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_eq_024), we get

$\\ \\frac{d\\lambda}{dc}|\_{i\\omega} = \\! - \\!\\left( \\frac{- i\\omega^{3}\\ \\frac{dA\_{3}}{dc} - \\frac{\\omega^{2}dA\_{2}}{dc} + \\frac{i\\omega dA\_{1}}{dc} + \\frac{dA\_{0}}{dc}}{- 4i\\omega^{3} - 3A\_{3}\\omega^{2} + 2A\_{2}i\\omega + A\_{1}} \\right)$ 

Hence ${Re}\\left( {\\frac{d\\lambda}{dc}|\_{i\\omega}} \\right) = - \\left( \\frac{\\left\\lbrack {A - 3A\_{3}\\omega^{2}} \\right\\rbrack\\left\\lbrack {\\frac{dA\_{0}}{dc} - \\omega^{2}\\frac{dA\_{2}}{dc}} \\right\\rbrack + \\left\\lbrack {2A\_{2}\\omega - 4\\omega^{3}} \\right\\rbrack\\left\\lbrack {\\omega^{3}\\frac{dA\_{3}}{dc} - \\omega\\frac{dA\_{1}}{dc}} \\right\\rbrack}{{\\lbrack A\_{1} - 3A\_{3}\\omega^{2}\\rbrack}^{2} + \\left\\lbrack {2A\_{2}\\omega - 4\\omega^{3}} \\right\\rbrack^{2}} \\right)$

**Theorem 15.15:** If we assume that “*c*” is the bifurcation parameter, then system (1) maintains the given Hopf bifurcation $\\left( {\\left\\lbrack {A\_{1} - 3A\_{3}\\omega^{2}} \\right\\rbrack\\left\\lbrack {\\frac{dA\_{0}}{dc} - \\omega^{2}\\frac{dA\_{2}}{dc}} \\right\\rbrack + \\left\\lbrack {2A\_{2}\\omega - 4\\omega^{3}} \\right\\rbrack\\!\\,\\left\\lbrack {\\omega^{3}\\frac{dA\_{3}}{dc} - \\omega\\frac{dA\_{1}}{dc}} \\right\\rbrack} \\right) \\neq 0.$

## 15.7 Discussions and Conclusions

There are some quite intriguing dynamics in an eco-epidemiology model with three prey and one predator as the sickness spreads to the third prey group. In this case, we imagined that all three preys develop logistically, with the exception of the third, which is incapable of procreating. Therefore, with the use of Maple and AI approaches, all of our significant analytical discoveries are quantitatively validated. The time-delayed system experiences a Hopf bifurcation at approximately *E*\* at *c* = *c*\*, taking time delay *c* as the bifurcation parameter.

Finally, take some control measure *Uτ*, which plays an important role in controlling population stability. This model will analyze the stability, which is shown in Table 15.1:

*   From [Figure 15.2](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_fig_002), we observed that the first prey *N*[1] belongs to the child age increases and becomes constant, and the second prey *N*[2] belongs to adult age and becomes constant due to lower immunity growth compared to the first prey.
    
*   From [Figure 15.3](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_fig_003), we find that the first prey *N*[1] and second prey *N*[2] becomes constant, but the third prey *N*[3] increases slowly because of infection by the predator *N*[4].
    
*   From [Figure 15.4](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_fig_004), we have shown that the third prey *N*[3] increases because of the control measure *Uτ* acting as a key role but the predator *N*[4] decreases.
    
*   From [Figure 15.5](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_fig_005), we find that the second prey *N*[2] goes to a constant, while the predator *N*[4] decreases.
    
*   From [Figure 15.6](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_fig_006), we observe that the first prey *N*[1] increases and then becomes constant, while the predator *N*[4] decreases.
    
*   From [Figure 15.7](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_fig_007), we find that the first prey *N*[1] and the second prey *N*[2] become a constant, and the third prey *N*[3] increases because of the parameter value of the control measure *Uτ* = 0.58315 so as to avoid the disease from spreading, while the predator *N*[4] diminishes instantly.
    

In our real-life situations, we compare this model by following the constant mentioned in *Uτ* as a preventive way to avoid the disease from spreading. Therefore, to avoid the spread of infection and disease, the predator spread in a third prey population could be reduced by applying the prevention and control measures described in [Figure 15.1](#9783111436050_039864.xhtml#b_9783111436180-015_fig_001), as *τ* control is recommended.
